# OxidePM

> OxidePM is an open-source process manager written in Rust, for Linux. It starts apps, restarts them when they crash, keeps their logs and brings them back after a reboot. The language runtimes, notifications, the web API, the terminal dashboard and Prometheus metrics are adapters. Licensed MIT or Apache-2.0.

Latest release: 0.4.0-rc.2. On Linux, the install script imports and enables the four bundled runtime adapters. macOS supports the built-in `cmd` runtime. The adapter launcher and sandbox are Linux-only in this release. Source: https://github.com/oxidekit/oxidepm.

This file holds every documentation page of oxidepm.com in Markdown. Each page also has its own `.md` address next to its HTML address.

---

# Install

Install OxidePM with the install script, a package, a prebuilt archive or from source.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/getting-started/install/

## Requirements

- Linux on x86_64 or ARM64, or macOS on Intel or Apple Silicon. macOS supports the built-in `cmd` runtime. The adapter launcher and sandbox are Linux-only in this release.
- Install the programs your apps need, such as Node.js, Python, Go or Rust.
- A Rust toolchain is required to build from source.

## The install script

*Install*

```sh
curl -fsSL https://oxidepm.com/install.sh | sh
```

The [install script](https://oxidepm.com/install.sh) installs the latest published release, 0.4.0-rc.2.

- Detects the platform with `uname`, looks up the latest release on GitHub and downloads its platform archive and `checksums.txt`.
- Checks the archive's SHA-256 against the entry for that exact filename in `checksums.txt`.
- Installs `oxidepm`, `oxidepmd` and `oxidepm-sandbox` into `/usr/local/bin`, using `sudo` when needed. Set `INSTALL_DIR` to install elsewhere.
- Copies the bundle into `share/oxidepm/adapters` under the installation prefix and checks the CLI version if `oxidepm` is on `PATH`.
- On Linux, imports and enables the runtimes offline with `oxidepm adapter import --bundled --tag runtime --enable --yes`. The CLI and daemon verify the catalog and the selected archives against the bundle's `SHA256SUMS`. If the import fails, the binaries stay installed and the script prints the command to retry.

## Other ways

The [Releases page](https://github.com/oxidekit/oxidepm/releases) has the archives and Debian packages:

| Platform | Architecture | Archive |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | x86_64 | `oxidepm-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` |
| Linux | ARM64 | `oxidepm-aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` |
| macOS | Intel | `oxidepm-x86_64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` |
| macOS | Apple Silicon | `oxidepm-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` |

For Homebrew and Arch Linux instructions, see the [OxidePM README](https://github.com/oxidekit/oxidepm/blob/prod/README.md#installation).

## Runtimes

The built-in `cmd` runtime runs an executable. The `runtime-node`, `runtime-python`, `runtime-go` and `runtime-rust` adapters provide `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `python`, `go`, `rust` and `cargo`. The release archive carries them under `share/oxidepm/adapters`. On Linux, import and enable them offline with:

```sh
oxidepm adapter import --bundled --tag runtime --enable --yes
```

On Linux, serving a runtime request requires its adapter to be imported and enabled. For optional adapters, see [Import and enable](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/import-and-enable/).

## From source

*Build*

```sh
git clone --branch v0.4.0-rc.2 https://github.com/oxidekit/oxidepm
cd oxidepm
cargo build --workspace --release
```

The binaries are in `target/release`. Install `oxidepm` and `oxidepmd` in the same directory on `PATH`. On Linux, place `oxidepm-sandbox` beside them. To add the bundled runtimes to a Linux source build, copy `share/oxidepm/adapters` from the release archive to the same path under your installation prefix and run the import command above.

## Check it

```sh
oxidepm --version
oxidepm status
```

If `status` reports that the daemon is down, `oxidepm start` starts it when you launch an app.

---

# Your first app

Start an app, look at it, read its logs and stop it.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/getting-started/first-app/

## Start an app

`oxidepm start` takes a file, a directory or a config file. It starts the daemon if it is not running, and the daemon keeps your app running after you close the terminal.

On Linux, use the bundled runtimes to start a script or project:

```sh
oxidepm start app.py            # a script: the runtime comes from its extension
oxidepm start ./my-project      # a directory: the runtime comes from the files in it
oxidepm start oxidepm.config.toml
```

OxidePM can pick a runtime from a script's extension (`.js`, `.py`, `.go`, `.rs`) or a project file (`package.json`, `Cargo.toml`, `go.mod`, `requirements.txt`). Use `--mode` to choose a runtime explicitly. See [Runtimes](https://oxidepm.com/docs/getting-started/install/#runtimes) for the bundled adapters.

macOS supports the built-in `cmd` runtime. The adapter launcher and sandbox are Linux-only in this release. To run a script with an interpreter installed on your `PATH`, specify the interpreter explicitly, for example `oxidepm start --mode cmd python3 -- app.py`.

A config file starts every app in it, as one batch. This one is the example used on these pages. It is the file the sample output below came from, with small stand-in programs for the real ones:

*oxidepm.config.toml*

```toml
[[apps]]
name = "db"
mode = "cmd"
script = "sleep"
args = ["100000"]
protected = true

[[apps]]
name = "api"
mode = "cmd"
script = "python3"
args = ["-m", "http.server", "18080", "--bind", "127.0.0.1"]
depends_on = ["db"]
ai_control = true

[apps.health_check]
http_url = "http://127.0.0.1:18080/"

[[apps]]
name = "web"
mode = "cmd"
script = "sleep"
args = ["100000"]
depends_on = ["api"]
ai_control = true
```

*Terminal output of oxidepm start with a config file*

```text
$ oxidepm start docs.config.toml
✓ Started db (id: 1)
✓ Started api (id: 2, waiting for its dependencies)
✓ Started web (id: 3, waiting for its dependencies)

Started 3 apps
```

An app that waits for its dependencies shows as `waiting`, and the start returns at once. `api` has a health check, so it stays `starting` until its first probe passes.

## Look at it

*Terminal output of oxidepm status while apps are starting*

```text
$ oxidepm status
╭────┬──────┬──────┬─────────┬───┬──────────┬──────┬─────┬────────╮
│ id │ name │ mode │ pid     │ ↺ │ status   │ cpu  │ mem │ uptime │
├────┼──────┼──────┼─────────┼───┼──────────┼──────┼─────┼────────┤
│  1 │ db   │ cmd  │ 1484325 │ 0 │ online   │ 0.0% │ 0B  │ 1s     │
│  2 │ api  │ cmd  │ 1484326 │ 0 │ starting │ 0.0% │ 0B  │ 1s     │
│  3 │ web  │ cmd  │ -       │ 0 │ waiting  │ 0.0% │ 0B  │ 0s     │
╰────┴──────┴──────┴─────────┴───┴──────────┴──────┴─────┴────────╯
```

The columns are `id`, `name`, `mode` (the runtime), `pid`, `↺` (restarts), `status`, `cpu`, `mem` and `uptime`. `online` is the status the table shows for an app that is running; `--json` calls it `running`. [All statuses](https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/restarts/).

`oxidepm status --more` adds the port, the working directory and the policy markers. `oxidepm show <name>` prints one app in detail. `oxidepm status --json` prints the table as JSON.

## Read its logs

```sh
oxidepm logs api            # the last 15 lines
oxidepm logs api -f         # follow
oxidepm logs api --lines 100 --grep "error"
```

`--out` shows only stdout and `--err` only stderr. [More on logs](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/logs/).

## Stop it

```sh
oxidepm stop api
oxidepm restart api
oxidepm delete api          # stop and remove it from the registry
oxidepm kill                # stop the daemon and every app
```

A selector is a name, an id, `all`, or `@tag`. A stopped app stays stopped and is not restarted by the daemon. `reload` is the same as `restart`: there is no zero-downtime reload.

---

# Survive a reboot

Save the app list, generate a boot unit and bring the apps back.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/getting-started/reboot/

## Save the list

```sh
oxidepm save
```

`save` writes `saved.json` in the data directory (`~/.oxidepm`, or the directory `OXIDEPM_HOME` names) from the apps that should be running. It refuses to replace a file that lists apps with an empty list, unless you pass `--force`. The file is written atomically with mode 0600.

## Bring the apps back

```sh
oxidepm resurrect
```

`resurrect` starts every app that should be running and is not up, and adds apps from `saved.json` that were deleted since. An app you stopped stays stopped. Apps are started in dependency order, and at most four build and spawn at once (the `launch_concurrency` setting), so a reboot does not run twenty builds together.

## Start the daemon at boot

```sh
oxidepm startup systemd     # or: launchd
```

This generates an autostart script for your init system. `oxidepm --dry-run startup` shows what would be written and writes nothing. The generated systemd unit has this shape (your user and paths will differ):

*oxidepmd.service*

```ini
[Unit]
Description=OxidePM Process Manager
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=deploy
ExecStart="/usr/local/bin/oxidepmd"
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=10
TimeoutStopSec=160
KillMode=mixed
Environment="HOME=/home/deploy"

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

`TimeoutStopSec` is the daemon's shutdown budget (`shutdown_budget_secs`, 120 seconds by default) plus 40 seconds, and `KillMode=mixed` makes systemd send the stop signal to the daemon alone and leave it time to stop the apps in order. Run `startup` again after you change the budget, to get the new value.

The daemon starts the apps that should be running when it starts at boot. On Linux, `pids.json` in the data directory lists the live app processes: if the daemon dies by SIGKILL, the next daemon kills what is still listed there before it starts anything. On macOS that recovery is not available, and the daemon logs a warning instead.

---

# Upgrade

Update to a newer release with `oxidepm update`, and what it checks.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/getting-started/upgrade/

## Update

```sh
oxidepm update                      # the latest release
oxidepm update --version 0.4.0-rc.2    # a specific version
```

`update` downloads the release archive for your platform and installs it. It is careful about it:

- The archive must match the SHA-256 in the release's `checksums.txt`. That is an integrity check. There is no release signing key yet, so authenticity is not checked.
- The asset is the one named exactly `oxidepm-<target>.tar.gz`, and it is unpacked safely.
- A running daemon is stopped, the files are replaced atomically with the old ones kept as `.pre-update`, and the new `oxidepm --version` is run. If that fails, everything is put back.
- An older version needs `--force`.

`oxidepm --dry-run update` downloads the archive into a private temporary directory, checks it against `checksums.txt`, unpacks it there, shows what it would replace and deletes the directory. Nothing is installed and no daemon is stopped.

The update installs the release's adapter bundle alongside the executables. On Linux, run `oxidepm adapter import --bundled --tag runtime --enable --yes` to import and enable the bundled runtimes. macOS supports the built-in `cmd` runtime. The adapter launcher and sandbox are Linux-only in this release.

## Keep the CLI and daemon together

The CLI and the daemon must come from the same release. A config file is sent to the daemon as one `StartBatch` request, so `oxidepm start <config file>` needs a daemon of the same release.

## State from older releases

When upgrading from 0.3.2, keep a copy of your app configuration and stop the old daemon before installing. The new daemon uses `state.db` and a versioned `saved.json`. Start your apps from their configs and run `oxidepm save` to record the new state.

---

# The config file

Where an app's settings live, which formats are read and how strictly.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/config-file/

## Writing one

A config file lists apps. It is a TOML file by default; YAML and JSON are read too, chosen by the file extension (`.toml`, `.yaml`, `.yml`, `.json`). The documented names are `oxidepm.config.toml` and `ecosystem.config.toml`, but any file name with a known extension works.

*oxidepm.config.toml*

```toml
[[apps]]
name = "api"
mode = "cargo"
cwd = "./api"
env = { RUST_LOG = "info" }
tags = ["backend"]

[[apps]]
name = "web"
mode = "npm"
script = "start"
cwd = "./web"
env_file = ".env"
instances = 2
port = 3000

[[apps]]
name = "worker"
mode = "node"
script = "worker.js"
max_restarts = 5
restart_delay = 2000
depends_on = ["api"]              # wait for the api to be running first
restart_cron = "0 4 * * *"        # restart daily at 4am UTC

log_max_size = "50mb"
log_max_files = 10
log_compress = true
```

The `cargo`, `npm` and `node` modes in this example are provided by the `runtime-rust` and `runtime-node` adapters that a release carries. With `mode = "cmd"` the app needs no adapter. See [Runtimes](https://oxidepm.com/docs/getting-started/install/#runtimes).

Start everything in it with:

```sh
oxidepm start oxidepm.config.toml
```

The file is sent to the daemon as one batch, so an app may be listed before the apps it depends on. Each app gets its own result: an app that cannot start does not stop the others, but the apps that depend on it are refused too.

## Checked strictly

A config file is checked when it is loaded, and nothing is started if it fails. A file that does not parse is reported with its name and the line of the problem; the other errors name the app, the key or the file they are about. These are all errors:

- an unknown key (a typo such as `restart_mode`, which is spelled `restart`),
- a bad cron expression or log size,
- a health check that is not exactly one of `http_url`, `tcp` or `script`,
- an `env_file` that does not exist,
- a `script` whose runtime cannot be inferred from its extension (set `mode`),
- the legacy app keys `watch`, `ignore` and `ignore_patterns`, which moved to the `watch` adapter,
- a dependency on an app that is not in the file or the registry, or a dependency cycle.

*Terminal output of oxidepm start with a config file that has an unknown key*

```text
$ oxidepm start bad.toml
Error: Config error: bad.toml: TOML parse error at line 5, column 1
  |
5 | restart_mode = "always"
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^
unknown field `restart_mode`, expected one of `name`, `mode`, `runtime`, `script`, `bin`, `cwd`, `args`, `env`, `env_file`, `restart_delay`, `max_restarts`, `max_restart_delay`, `stable_uptime`, `crash_window`, `kill_timeout`, `no_autorestart`, `instances`, `port`, `port_range`, `health_check`, `max_memory_mb`, `hooks`, `tags`, `max_uptime_secs`, `restart`, `binary`, `depends_on`, `depends_timeout`, `depends_fail_open`, `restart_cron`, `log_max_size`, `log_max_files`, `log_compress`, `adapters`, `protected`, `ai_control`
```

## The daemon keeps its own copy

A config file is read only by `oxidepm start <file>`. The daemon keeps the spec an app was started with: `restart` and `reload` reuse it, and `start` of an app that is already up is refused with `E_APP_EXISTS`. To apply a changed file, stop the app and start the file again. An app that is at rest takes the new spec.

A config file has no key for the startup delay or for `env_inherit`. Those are `--delay` and `--env-inherit` of a single `start`.

## Reserved tables

The top-level tables `adapters` and `policy` are reserved and must be empty. Use `[apps.adapters.<name>]` for per-app adapter options. For example, `[apps.adapters.watch]` opts an app in to [file watching](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/other-commands/#file-watching).

The keys of an app are on the next page.

---

# Apps

Every key an app can have in a config file.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/apps/

Every key an app can have in a config file. Times are in the unit the key names: `_ms` and the restart and kill delays are milliseconds, `_secs`, `stable_uptime` and `crash_window` are seconds.

## What to run

- `name` (string): The app's name. Required. A name is also what a selector matches, so it is limited in charset and length (a cluster name to 59 characters).
- `mode` (string, alias: runtime): How to run it: `cmd` (any program, the only runtime in the core), or a runtime an enabled adapter provides: `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn` (`runtime-node`), `python` (`runtime-python`), `go` (`runtime-go`), `rust` and `cargo` (`runtime-rust`). An app whose runtime adapter is missing is refused with `E_ADAPTER_MISSING` and the command that imports it. If you leave it out, a `script` gets its mode from its extension, and the file is refused if that is not possible.
- `script` (string): What to run. For `cmd` it is the program; for `npm`, `pnpm` and `yarn` the name of the package script; for `node` and `python` the file.
- `bin` (string): The binary name, for `cargo`.
- `binary` (string): The path to a binary, as an alternative to `script` or `bin`.
- `args` (list of strings, default: none): Arguments passed to the program.
- `cwd` (string): The working directory.

## Environment and tags

- `env` (table, default: empty): Environment variables for the app, for example `env = { RUST_LOG = "info" }`.
- `env_file` (string): A file of `KEY=VALUE` lines. A missing file is an error.
- `tags` (list of strings, default: none): Group apps, and select them with `@tag`.

## Restarts

- `restart` (string, default: "on-crash"): `on-crash`, `always` or `never`. See [Restarts and states](/docs/configuration/restarts/).
- `no_autorestart` (boolean, default: false): Turn automatic restarts off.
- `restart_delay` (number, default: 500): Milliseconds before the first restart. It doubles for every crash in a row.
- `max_restart_delay` (number, default: 60000): The cap on that delay, in milliseconds.
- `max_restarts` (number, default: 15): More than this many restarts inside `crash_window` end the app `errored`.
- `crash_window` (number, default: 600): Seconds. See `max_restarts`.
- `stable_uptime` (number, default: 60): A run this long, in seconds, starts the delay over.
- `kill_timeout` (number, default: 3000): Milliseconds the app has to exit after the stop signal.

## Dependencies, limits and schedules

- `depends_on` (list of app names, default: none): Apps that must be running before this one starts. See [Dependencies](/docs/configuration/dependencies/).
- `depends_timeout` (seconds, default: 60): How long to wait for them, from 1 to 3600.
- `depends_fail_open` (boolean, default: false): Launch anyway, with a warning, when the wait times out. Discouraged.
- `max_memory_mb` (number): Restart the app when it is over this resident size. See [Limits and cron](/docs/configuration/limits-and-cron/).
- `max_uptime_secs` (number): Restart the app after this many seconds of uptime.
- `restart_cron` (string): A cron expression for scheduled restarts. Five fields, UTC; Sunday is 0 or 7.

## Clusters

- `instances` (number, default: 1): How many instances, up to 256. See [Clusters](/docs/configuration/clusters/).
- `port` (number): The base port. Instance `i` gets `port + i`.
- `port_range` (table): `{ start = 3000, end = 3010 }`. The range must hold every instance. `port` and `port_range` together are refused.

## Checks, hooks and logs

- `health_check` (table): Exactly one of `http_url`, `tcp` or `script`, plus optional settings. See [Health checks](/docs/configuration/health-checks/).
- `hooks` (table): `on_start`, `on_stop`, `on_restart`, `on_crash`, `on_error`. See [Environment and hooks](/docs/configuration/environment-and-hooks/).
- `log_max_size` (string, default: "10mb"): Rotate a log file at this size, for example `"50mb"`.
- `log_max_files` (number, default: 5): How many rotated files to keep.
- `log_compress` (boolean, default: false): Compress rotated files with gzip.

## Safety markers

- `protected` (boolean, default: false): Read-only for AI actors and other non-human callers. See [Protected apps](/docs/ai-safety/protected-apps/).
- `ai_control` (boolean, default: false): AI actors may stop, restart and reload the app. They can never start or delete it.

## Adapter options

- `adapters` (table): Per-app adapter options. Each adapter name maps to a table. Use `[apps.adapters.watch]` to opt in to [file watching](/docs/commands/other-commands/#file-watching), or `[apps.adapters.ui-web]` to opt in to [web API lifecycle controls](/docs/commands/other-commands/#web).

---

# Restarts and states

Restart policy, backoff, the crash-loop breaker and the states an app moves through.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/restarts/

## States

`oxidepm status` shows one of these for each app. In `--json` output `online` is called `running`.

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `waiting` | A start was accepted and waits for `depends_on` or a startup delay. |
| `building` | Building from source. |
| `starting` | Spawned, and with a health check, until the first probe has passed. |
| `online` | Running. |
| `unhealthy` | Alive, but the health check failed `retries` times in a row. |
| `backoff` | Crashed. An automatic restart is scheduled. |
| `stopping` | Shutting down. |
| `stopped` | Stopped by a person. It stays stopped. |
| `errored` | A crash loop, a launch that failed, an exit that is not restarted, or a failed dependency. |

A `stop` acts on every state except `stopped` and `errored`: it also cancels a pending start, a build and a pending restart. A `start` of an app that is not at rest (anything but `stopped` and `errored`, `backoff` and `waiting` included) is refused with `E_APP_EXISTS` and changes nothing.

## The restart policy

A crashed app waits in `backoff` and is restarted automatically unless `--no-autorestart` or the config key `restart` says otherwise. `restart` is one of:

- `on-crash` (the default): a non-zero exit or a death by a signal is restarted. An exit with code 0 is not, and leaves the app `errored`.
- `always`: any exit is restarted.
- `never`: nothing is restarted.

A restart caused by a memory or uptime limit, by a health check with `action = "restart"`, or by a launch that failed during a restart ignores both settings. A manual `stop` is never restarted automatically.

## Backoff and the crash-loop breaker

The delay before the first restart is `restart_delay` (500 ms by default) and doubles for every crash in a row, up to `max_restart_delay` (60 000 ms). A run of `stable_uptime` seconds (60 by default) starts the delay over.

More than `max_restarts` restarts (15 by default) inside any `crash_window` seconds (600 by default) are a crash loop. The app ends `errored` and stays `errored` until a person starts it. `start` and `restart` by hand give the app a fresh budget.

A launch that fails during an automatic restart (the program is gone, a log file cannot be opened) is one more attempt with a longer delay, not the end.

*Terminal output: an app in a crash loop, then its logs*

```text
$ oxidepm status
╭────┬────────┬──────┬─────┬───┬─────────┬──────┬─────┬────────╮
│ id │ name   │ mode │ pid │ ↺ │ status  │ cpu  │ mem │ uptime │
├────┼────────┼──────┼─────┼───┼─────────┼──────┼─────┼────────┤
│  1 │ mailer │ cmd  │ -   │ 3 │ errored │ 0.0% │ 0B  │ 0s     │
╰────┴────────┴──────┴─────┴───┴─────────┴──────┴─────┴────────╯
$ oxidepm logs mailer --lines 3
[2026-10-31 04:11:47.153] cannot reach smtp
[2026-10-31 04:11:47.559] cannot reach smtp
[2026-10-31 04:11:48.362] cannot reach smtp
```

Here the app was started with `max_restarts = 3` and `restart_delay = 200`. The `↺` column counts restarts. Read the logs before you restart an errored app: the cause is usually there.

## Reload is a restart

`oxidepm reload` is the same as `restart`: the process is stopped and started again. There is no zero-downtime reload.

---

# Dependencies

Use `depends_on` to make an app wait for the apps it needs. A wait that fails closed.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/dependencies/

## Declare a dependency

List the names of the apps this one needs. Here `api` needs the database, and `web` needs `api`.

*oxidepm.config.toml*

```toml
[[apps]]
name = "db"
mode = "cmd"
script = "postgres"
args = ["-D", "/srv/pg/data"]

[[apps]]
name = "api"
mode = "cmd"
script = "./target/release/api"
depends_on = ["db"]

[apps.health_check]
http_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/health"

[[apps]]
name = "web"
mode = "npm"
script = "start"
depends_on = ["api"]
```

## What happens at start

The checks run when the app is started:

- A name that is not registered is refused at once (`E_DEPENDENCY_MISSING`), and so is a cycle (`E_DEPENDENCY_CYCLE`, and the message names it).
- A single `start` of an app whose dependency is `stopped` or `errored` right now is refused with the remedy (`E_DEPENDENCY_FAILED`).
- Otherwise the start is accepted and the app shows `waiting` until every dependency is `online`. The start returns at once and nothing else is blocked. A `stop` cancels the wait.

*Terminal output of oxidepm start: api and web wait for their dependencies*

```text
$ oxidepm start docs.config.toml
✓ Started db (id: 1)
✓ Started api (id: 2, waiting for its dependencies)
✓ Started web (id: 3, waiting for its dependencies)

Started 3 apps
```

If a dependency has a health check, it is `online` only once its first probe has passed. Until then it is `starting`, and the apps that wait for it keep waiting.

*Terminal output of refused starts*

```text
$ oxidepm start api-only.toml
✗ Failed to start api: dependency 'db' is stopped; start it first

Started: 0, Failed: 1
Error: 1 of 1 apps failed to start (started: none; failed: api)

$ oxidepm start cycle.toml
Error: Config error: depends_on cycle: a -> b -> a
```

## The wait fails closed

A dependency that ends `errored`, or is deleted, fails the dependent at once. So does `depends_timeout` (1 to 3600 seconds, 60 by default): the app ends `errored` with the reason `dependency 'db' not running after 60s` (`E_DEPENDENCY_TIMEOUT`) and is never launched. It does not start anyway and fail in a confusing way.

`depends_fail_open = true` turns that timeout into a warning and a launch. It is discouraged.

Once an app is running, a later failure of its dependency does not touch it.

## When the wait applies

The wait applies to a start or restart by hand of an app that was at rest. A `restart` of an app that is up, and every automatic restart (crash, limit, cron, health), skip it: a crashed app comes back through the normal backoff even while its dependency is down.

An app that waits holds no build slot. At most `launch_concurrency` apps (4 by default, a [daemon setting](https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/daemon-settings/)) build and spawn at once.

## Stop order

`stop all`, and a stop by tag, stops dependents before their dependencies, layer by layer. The daemon's shutdown does the same within its time budget. A `stop` of one app stops that app only: its dependents keep running.

*Terminal output of oxidepm stop all --dry-run*

```text
$ oxidepm stop all --dry-run
ℹ Dry run of 'stop': this is what would happen. Nothing was changed.
  stop  web [step 0]  status running
  stop  api [step 1]  status running
  stop  db [step 2]  status running
```

`--dry-run` shows the order without stopping anything. `restart db --dry-run` on a running app says the dependency gate is skipped because the app is up.

## Fields

- `depends_on` (list of app names, default: none): Apps that must be running before this one starts. A name must be in the same file or already registered.
- `depends_timeout` (seconds, default: 60): How long to wait for them, from 1 to 3600, before the app ends `errored`.
- `depends_fail_open` (boolean, default: false): Launch anyway, with a warning, when the wait times out.

---

# Health checks

HTTP, TCP and script checks, and what the daemon does when one fails.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/health-checks/

## Add a check

```sh
oxidepm start ./server --health-check http://localhost:3000/health   # HTTP
oxidepm start ./server --health-check ./check-health.sh              # a script
```

In a config file a check is a table with exactly one of `http_url`, `tcp` or `script`:

*oxidepm.config.toml*

```toml
[[apps]]
name = "api"
mode = "cmd"
script = "./target/release/api"

[apps.health_check]
http_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/health"
expected_status = [200, 204]
interval_secs = 30
retries = 3
action = "restart"
```

## How a check runs

An app with a check is `starting` until its first probe has passed. The first probe runs `start_period_secs` after the launch, then one runs every `interval_secs`. A probe times out after `timeout_secs`.

- An HTTP check passes on status 200 unless `expected_status` lists others. It does not follow redirects: a 301 is a failure unless it is listed.
- A `tcp` check (`"host:port"`) passes when the connection is accepted.
- A `script` check runs in the app's directory, as `sh -c`, with the same limited environment as a hook.

After `retries` failures in a row the app is `unhealthy`, the `on_error` hook fires once for that streak, and the `health_check` notification is sent if the notifier adapter is enabled. It goes back to `online` when a probe passes again.

The child is left alone unless the check sets `action = "restart"`, which replaces it with an automatic restart.

## Fields

- `http_url` (string): The URL to request. Exactly one of `http_url`, `tcp` and `script` is required.
- `tcp` (string): `"host:port"`.
- `script` (string): A script or command.
- `expected_status` (list of numbers, default: [200]): The HTTP status codes that count as healthy.
- `interval_secs` (number, default: 30): Seconds between probes.
- `timeout_secs` (number, default: 5): Seconds before a probe fails. 5, or the interval if that is shorter.
- `retries` (number, default: 3): Failures in a row before the app is `unhealthy`.
- `start_period_secs` (number, default: 5): Seconds after the launch before the first probe.
- `action` (string, default: "notify"): `notify` leaves the child alone. `restart` replaces it.

---

# Limits and cron

Restart an app over a memory or uptime limit, or on a cron schedule.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/limits-and-cron/

## Memory and uptime limits

```sh
oxidepm start ./app --max-memory 512 --max-uptime 24h
```

In a config file the keys are `max_memory_mb` and `max_uptime_secs`. An app over a limit is replaced: the daemon stops its process group, waits the restart delay and starts it again with the same plan.

- A limit restart ignores the `restart` setting and `no_autorestart`.
- A run of 5 seconds or more never counts towards `max_restarts`, so a periodic restart (`--max-uptime 24h`) cannot end in a crash loop. A limit that fires within 5 seconds of every start is counted like a crash, and the breaker ends it.
- A `stop` or `restart` by hand always wins over a limit restart that is still on its way.
- Memory is sampled every 2 seconds from the resident size of the app's first process, the one the daemon started. With `npm start` that is `npm`, not the `node` child under it, so give a wrapped app the limit of the wrapper, or start the program directly.
- Uptime counts from the launch.

`--max-uptime` takes a duration such as `30m`, `1h`, `24h`, `1d` or `1h30m`; a plain number is seconds.

## Cron restarts

*oxidepm.config.toml*

```toml
[[apps]]
name = "worker"
mode = "cmd"
script = "./worker"
restart_cron = "0 4 * * *"    # every day at 04:00 UTC
```

The expression has the usual five fields, in UTC, and Sunday is 0 or 7. A bad expression is an error when the file is loaded. A scheduled restart ignores the `restart` setting, like a limit restart, and is recorded as the daemon's own work (`system:cron`) in the audit log.

---

# Clusters

Run several instances of one app, with a port for each.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/clusters/

```sh
oxidepm start ./server -i 4 --port 3000
```

or in a config file:

*oxidepm.config.toml*

```toml
[[apps]]
name = "web"
mode = "node"
script = "server.js"
instances = 4
port = 3000
```

## The shape of a cluster

A cluster is a parent (`web`, with no process) and one app per instance (`web-0`, `web-1`, and so on). There are at most 256 instances. Instance `i` gets port `port + i`, or the start of `port_range` plus `i`. The range must hold every instance, and `port` and `port_range` together are refused.

## Starting and stopping

- The cluster is created all at once. A name that is already taken (`web-1` included) refuses the start with `E_APP_EXISTS` and writes nothing. If an instance cannot launch on the first start, the whole cluster is deleted again and the instance's error is returned.
- Starting a cluster that exists starts only the instances that are at rest: after `stop web-1`, `start web` brings back `web-1` and leaves the others running.
- The number of instances cannot change (`E_INVALID_SPEC`). Delete and recreate. That includes starting an existing single app with more than one instance, or an existing cluster with one.
- `delete web` removes the parent and all instance rows in one transaction, before any instance is stopped.
- A tag or `all` that matches a cluster and its instances acts on the cluster once. `web-1` by name acts on that instance only.

## Policy

The markers `protected` and `ai_control` of a cluster apply to every instance. An instance created later takes the markers of its cluster. An instance can be set on its own, but it counts as protected when its cluster is, and as open to AI control only when both are.

---

# Log files

Where an app's output goes, and how the files rotate.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/log-files/

## Where the logs are

The daemon captures each app's output in its data directory (`~/.oxidepm/logs`, or under `OXIDEPM_HOME`):

```text
logs/
├── api-out.log      # stdout
├── api-err.log      # stderr
└── api-hooks.log    # output of the app's event hooks
```

Every line is timestamped when the daemon writes it. Read them with `oxidepm logs <name>`, [described here](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/logs/).

## Rotation

Logs rotate by size, per app. The defaults are 10 MB per file, 5 files, and no compression. Change them in the config file:

*oxidepm.config.toml*

```toml
[[apps]]
name = "api"
mode = "cmd"
script = "./api"
log_max_size = "50mb"
log_max_files = 10
log_compress = true
```

`log_max_size` accepts values such as `"10mb"`, `"500kb"` or a number of bytes, and a bad value is an error when the file is loaded. `log_compress` compresses rotated files with gzip.

## Truncating

`oxidepm flush <selector>` truncates the active log files of an app. Rotated files stay. A file that cannot be emptied is reported for that app. The contents are lost, so read the logs before you flush them: a crashed app's logs are the evidence of why it crashed.

---

# Environment and hooks

What environment an app gets, how secrets are shown, and event hooks.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/environment-and-hooks/

## The environment an app gets

An app does not get the daemon's environment. It gets:

1. `PATH`, `HOME`, `USER`, `LOGNAME`, `SHELL`, `LANG`, `LC_*`, `TZ` and `TMPDIR`,
2. then `--env` (`env` in a config file) and `--env-file` (`env_file`),
3. and `OPM_APP_ID` and `OPM_APP_NAME` from the daemon (`OPM_INSTANCE_ID` for a cluster instance).

`--env-inherit` gives the app the daemon's whole environment instead. That is the environment of the daemon, not of the shell that ran `oxidepm start`. Build steps (`cargo build`, `rustc`) always get the daemon's environment.

## Secrets are not shown

`status`, `show`, `describe` and `env list` do not show environment values. The daemon replaces every value with `<redacted>`, and keeps the keys visible. Hook and health-check scripts show as `<set>`. `oxidepm show <name> --reveal` is the one way to see them, and the daemon writes a line to its log each time it is asked. It is a dangerous request, so an AI actor cannot make it.

Command arguments, URLs, logs, other command output and config files are not scrubbed. Keep tokens out of them: use `env_file` or environment variables.

`oxidepm env set` and `env unset` are refused. The daemon has no request that changes the environment of a saved app. Pass `--env KEY=VALUE` when starting the app, or set `env` in the config file and start the file again.

*Terminal output of oxidepm env list*

```text
$ oxidepm env list api
api: no environment variables set
```

## Event hooks

```sh
oxidepm start ./app \
  --on-start   "./notify.sh started" \
  --on-stop    "./notify.sh stopped" \
  --on-crash   "./notify.sh crashed" \
  --on-restart "./notify.sh restarted"
```

In a config file the table is `hooks`, with the same four keys and a fifth, `on_error`, which runs when the app ends `errored` or turns `unhealthy`.

A hook runs as `sh -c` in its own process group and is killed with everything it started after 30 seconds. Its output is appended to `logs/<name>-hooks.log`. It gets `PATH`, `HOME` and a few other basics from the daemon, the app's own `env`, and these variables, where they apply: `OPM_APP_ID`, `OPM_APP_NAME`, `OPM_EVENT`, `OPM_PID`, `OPM_EXIT_CODE`, `OPM_REASON` and `OPM_RESTARTS`. The daemon's other variables are not passed on, not even with `--env-inherit`.

---

# Daemon settings

The optional daemon.toml and the files in the data directory.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/daemon-settings/

## daemon.toml

`daemon.toml` in the data directory holds the daemon's own settings. The file is optional. An unknown key, or a value out of range, keeps the daemon from starting, and the error names it.

- `shutdown_budget_secs` (number, default: 120): Seconds the daemon spends stopping its apps on shutdown, from 10 to 900. The apps are stopped in dependency layers and the budget is shared between the layers. `oxidepm startup` uses it for `TimeoutStopSec`.
- `launch_concurrency` (number, default: 4): How many apps may build and spawn at once, from 1 to 64.
- `agent_socket` (boolean, default: true): Bind `agent.sock`, the socket whose every connection is an AI agent. See [Agent connections](/docs/ai-safety/agent-connections/).
- `reuse_plan` (boolean, default: true): An app whose runtime an adapter provides keeps the launch plan the adapter made, and a resurrect at boot or an automatic launch may start from it when the app, the adapter and its executable are unchanged: at once if the plan had no build steps, otherwise only when the adapter cannot be asked, and then with a warning. `false` always asks the adapter. A start or restart by a person never uses a stored plan.

## The data directory

Everything is in `~/.oxidepm`. The `OXIDEPM_HOME` environment variable names another directory.

```text
~/.oxidepm/
├── daemon.sock     # the CLI's socket (mode 0600)
├── agent.sock      # the socket for AI agents; every connection is class ai
├── oxidepmd.lock   # held by the running daemon: one daemon per home
├── daemon.toml     # optional daemon settings
├── state.db        # SQLite: full app specs and the two policy markers
├── daemon.log      # what the daemon wrote to stderr while it started (fatal startup errors)
├── daemon.log.DATE # the daemon's log, one file a day, the last 7 days kept
├── saved.json      # the saved process list
├── pids.json       # live app processes
├── audit/          # audit.jsonl and audit-security.jsonl
├── adapters.db     # SQLite: installed adapters, grants and consent (with -wal and -shm files while it is open)
├── adapter-pids.json # live adapter processes
├── adapters/       # installed adapters and their state (index, installed, staging, state, trash, verbs.json)
├── repos/          # git clones, created when first used
└── logs/           # app logs
```

## The sockets

The CLI and the daemon talk over `daemon.sock`, with mode 0600. The daemon drops connections from any other user. `OXIDEPM_SOCKET` names another socket for the CLI. A request is one line of JSON in an envelope that carries the protocol version (2) and a request id, and the answer is one line. A line may be up to 10 MiB, and a connection that sends nothing for 5 minutes is closed.

`agent.sock` is tighter: lines of at most 1 MiB, at most 32 connections at once, and a connection that is idle for 60 seconds is closed.

---

# Overview

The core commands, selectors and global flags, the commands and runtimes that adapters provide, and what you see when one is missing.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/overview/

## Core commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `start <target>` | Start a process, or every app of a config file (sent as one batch). |
| `start <target> --check` | Run preflight using the `check` adapter before starting a single file or project. |
| `stop <selector>` | Stop apps. |
| `restart <selector>` | Hard restart apps. Also starts an app that is at rest. |
| `reload <selector>` | The same as `restart`. There is no zero-downtime reload. |
| `delete <selector>` | Stop apps and remove them from the registry. |
| `status [--more\|--daemon]` | The status table. `--more` adds port, working directory and policy markers. `--daemon` shows the daemon itself. |
| `show <name> [--reveal]` | One app in detail. `--reveal` also prints environment values and hook scripts. |
| `logs <name> [-f]` | Read or follow logs. |
| `flush <selector>` | Truncate the active log files. |
| `describe <name>` | Show the command that would run for an app that is already registered, without starting anything. |
| `policy set <selector>` | Change the `protected` and `ai_control` markers of running apps. |
| `audit` | Read the audit log. |
| `save [--force]`, `resurrect` | Write and restore the list of apps that should run. |
| `startup [systemd\|launchd]` | Generate an autostart script. |
| `ping` | Check that the daemon is alive. |
| `kill` | Stop the daemon and every app. |
| `env list` | The keys of an app's environment. |
| `update [--version X] [--force]` | Update to a release. |
| `backup`, `restore <file>` | Export and restore the config and process list. |
| `adapter` | Find, import, enable and manage adapters. |
| `completions <shell>`, `man` | Shell completions and the man page. |

## Provided by adapters

On Linux, [import and enable the adapter](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/import-and-enable/#build-an-optional-adapter) to use its commands.

| Command | Adapter | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `notify` | [notifier](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/notifier/#the-notify-command) | Show, test and configure notifications to Telegram, Discord, Slack and webhooks. |
| `web`, `web status`, `web new-key` | `ui-web` | The web API and its WebSocket. See [web](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/other-commands/#web). |
| `monit` | `ui-tui` | The terminal dashboard, a session command that runs on your terminal. See [monit](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/other-commands/#monit-and-top). |
| `check [target]` | `check` | Check project readiness. |
| `init [dir]` | `init` | Generate a starter config file. |
| `git-start <url>` | `git-start` | Clone or update a repository and start it. |
| `deploy <host>`, `diff <host>` | `deploy` | Deploy over SSH and inspect the remote checkout. |

The [exporter-prometheus](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/exporter-prometheus/) service serves `/metrics`. The [`watch` service](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/other-commands/#file-watching) restarts opted-in apps when files change.

When an adapter is not installed, the command is refused with exit code 2 and the message names the adapter:

*Terminal output of oxidepm notify when the notifier is not installed*

```text
$ oxidepm notify status
error: unrecognized subcommand 'notify'

Usage: oxidepm [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

For more information, try '--help'.

'notify' is provided by the adapter 'notifier', which is not installed.
Install it with: oxidepm adapter import notifier   (see: oxidepm adapter list --available)
```

The import hint uses the signed-index form. This release has no configured network catalog, so use the [pinned archive instructions](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/import-and-enable/#build-an-optional-adapter).

## Runtimes

The core runs one runtime itself: `cmd`, which runs any program with its arguments. The language runtimes are adapters, and a release carries them:

| Runtime names | Adapter |
|---|---|
| `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn` | `runtime-node` |
| `python` | `runtime-python` |
| `go` | `runtime-go` |
| `rust`, `cargo` | `runtime-rust` |

On Linux, the install script runs `oxidepm adapter import --bundled --tag runtime --enable --yes` after installing the release bundle. See [Runtimes](https://oxidepm.com/docs/getting-started/install/#runtimes) for manual installs. Starting an app whose runtime is missing fails and creates nothing:

*Terminal output of oxidepm start when the runtime adapter is not enabled*

```text
$ oxidepm start /srv/app/app.js
✗ runtime 'node' is provided by the adapter 'runtime-node', which is not enabled. Run: oxidepm adapter import runtime-node --enable
Error: runtime 'node' is provided by the adapter 'runtime-node', which is not enabled. Run: oxidepm adapter import runtime-node --enable
```

The command in the message is the one for a missing adapter. If the adapter is installed but off, it says `Run: oxidepm adapter enable runtime-node` instead. The error code is `E_ADAPTER_MISSING`.

Still in the core: `top`, a live resource monitor.

## Selectors

A selector is an app name, an id, `all`, or `@tag` for a group. A cluster (`web`) and its instances (`web-0`, `web-1`) are selected as one when a tag or `all` matches both. An AI actor may not use `all` or a tag with `stop`, `restart` or `reload`.

## Global flags

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--json` | Print machine-readable output instead of tables. |
| `--dry-run` | Say what the command would do and change nothing. |
| `-v` | More logging (`-vv`, `-vvv`). |

## Environment variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `OXIDEPM_HOME` | Use this data directory instead of `~/.oxidepm`. |
| `OXIDEPM_SOCKET` | The socket the CLI talks to. |
| `OXIDEPM_ACTOR` | The actor the CLI claims to be, such as `ai:assistant`. A claim can only make a request stricter. |

---

# start, stop, restart

Start an app or a config file, stop it, restart it, reload it and delete it.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/start-stop-restart/

## start

```sh
oxidepm start app.js
oxidepm start ./my-project --max-memory 512
oxidepm start oxidepm.config.toml
oxidepm start ./server -i 4 --port 3000
```

`start` takes a file, a directory, or a config file. The daemon is started if it is not running. A config file starts every app in it, and each app gets its own result.

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-n, --name <name>` | The app's name. |
| `--mode <runtime>` | Force the runtime (alias `--runtime`): `cmd`, which is in the core, or one an adapter provides: `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `cargo`, `rust`, `python` and `go` come from the runtime adapters. |
| `--script <name>` | The package script, for `npm`, `pnpm` and `yarn`. |
| `--bin <name>` | The binary, for `cargo`. |
| `--cwd <dir>` | The working directory. |
| `--env KEY=VALUE` | An environment variable. Repeatable. |
| `--env-file <file>` | An environment file. |
| `--env-inherit` | Give the app the daemon's whole environment. |
| `--tag <tag>` | A tag for grouping. Repeatable. |
| `-i, --instances <n>` | Cluster mode, from 1 to 256. |
| `--port <n>` | The base port. Instance `i` gets `port + i`. |
| `--delay <ms>` | Wait before starting the process. |
| `--restart-delay <ms>` | Delay before the first restart. |
| `--max-restarts <n>` | Restarts before the app ends `errored`. |
| `--kill-timeout <ms>` | Time to exit after the stop signal. |
| `--no-autorestart` | Turn automatic restarts off. |
| `--max-memory <MB>`, `--max-uptime <duration>` | Limits. See [Limits and cron](https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/limits-and-cron/). |
| `--health-check <url or script>` | An http(s) URL or a script. |
| `--on-start`, `--on-stop`, `--on-restart`, `--on-crash` | Event hooks. |
| `--protected`, `--ai-control` | The policy markers. |
| `--check` | Run preflight via the `check` adapter before starting a file or directory. Requires the enabled adapter. |
| `-- <args>` | Arguments passed to the program. |

Use [`git-start <url>`](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/other-commands/#git-start) to start from Git. Set [`[apps.adapters.watch]`](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/other-commands/#file-watching) for file watching. To apply project fixes, run `oxidepm check <target> --fix` separately. Run `oxidepm check` separately before starting a config file, too.

## stop, restart, reload, delete

```sh
oxidepm stop api
oxidepm restart api
oxidepm reload api
oxidepm delete api
```

- `stop` stops the app. It stays stopped and is not restarted automatically. With several apps (`all`, a tag), dependents are stopped before their dependencies.
- `restart` stops and starts the app again. It also starts an app that is at rest.
- `reload` is the same as `restart`.
- `delete` stops the app and removes it from the registry and the database.

*Terminal output of oxidepm restart*

```text
$ oxidepm restart web
✓ Restarted 1 process(es)
```

A `start` of an app that is not at rest is refused with `E_APP_EXISTS` and changes nothing. These commands take [`--dry-run`](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/dry-run/), except `start --check`.

---

# status and show

Read what is running: the table, the extra columns, one app in detail and the daemon itself.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/status/

## status

*Terminal output of oxidepm status*

```text
$ oxidepm status
╭────┬──────┬──────┬─────────┬───┬────────┬──────┬───────┬────────╮
│ id │ name │ mode │ pid     │ ↺ │ status │ cpu  │ mem   │ uptime │
├────┼──────┼──────┼─────────┼───┼────────┼──────┼───────┼────────┤
│  1 │ db   │ cmd  │ 1484325 │ 0 │ online │ 0.0% │ 2.5M  │ 5s     │
│  2 │ api  │ cmd  │ 1484326 │ 0 │ online │ 0.0% │ 22.2M │ 5s     │
│  3 │ web  │ cmd  │ 1485319 │ 0 │ online │ 0.0% │ 0B    │ 0s     │
╰────┴──────┴──────┴─────────┴───┴────────┴──────┴───────┴────────╯
```

The columns are:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | The app's id. |
| `name` | The name. |
| `mode` | The runtime. |
| `pid` | The process id, or `-` when it is not running. |
| `↺` | Restarts. |
| `status` | One of the [states](https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/restarts/). The table calls a running app `online`. |
| `cpu`, `mem` | Sampled from the app's first process. |
| `uptime` | Time since the launch. |

## status --more

*Terminal output of oxidepm status --more*

```text
$ oxidepm status --more
╭────┬──────┬──────┬─────────┬───┬────────┬──────┬─────────────────────┬────────┬────────────╮
│ id │ name │ mode │ pid     │ ↺ │ status │ port │ cwd                 │ uptime │ policy     │
├────┼──────┼──────┼─────────┼───┼────────┼──────┼─────────────────────┼────────┼────────────┤
│  1 │ db   │ cmd  │ 1484325 │ 0 │ online │ -    │ …/shopfront/current │ 5s     │ protected  │
│  2 │ api  │ cmd  │ 1484326 │ 0 │ online │ -    │ …/shopfront/current │ 5s     │ ai-control │
│  3 │ web  │ cmd  │ 1485319 │ 0 │ online │ -    │ …/shopfront/current │ 0s     │ ai-control │
╰────┴──────┴──────┴─────────┴───┴────────┴──────┴─────────────────────┴────────┴────────────╯
```

`--more` swaps `cpu` and `mem` for `port` and `cwd` and adds `policy`, which is `-`, `protected`, `ai-control`, or both. The working directory is shortened from the left.

## status --daemon

*Terminal output of oxidepm status --daemon*

```text
$ oxidepm status --daemon
audit log:    ok
agent socket: bound
sandbox:      landlock abi 10 (restricts unix connect), seccomp, ptrace_scope 1 (launcher installed)
```

`--daemon` shows how the daemon itself is: whether the audit log is `ok` or `degraded`, whether the agent socket is bound, what the [sandbox](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/sandbox/) can enforce on this machine, the state of each enabled adapter, and warnings, for example about an app whose runtime adapter is not enabled.

## show

```sh
oxidepm show api
oxidepm show api --reveal
```

`show` prints one app in detail: its state, command, working directory, arguments and last exit code. Environment values show as `<redacted>` and scripts as `<set>`. `--reveal` prints them, and the daemon writes a line to its log each time. It is a dangerous request, so an AI actor cannot make it.

`describe <name>` takes the name or id of an app that is already registered, and shows the command that would run for it, without starting anything. It does not take a file or a command to be started.

---

# logs and flush

Read, follow and filter an app's logs, and truncate them.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/logs/

## logs

```sh
oxidepm logs api                      # the last 15 lines
oxidepm logs api -f                   # follow
oxidepm logs api --lines 100
oxidepm logs api --err                # only stderr
oxidepm logs api --grep "timeout|refused"
```

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-f, --follow` | Follow the output. |
| `--lines <n>` | How many lines to show. 15 by default. |
| `--out`, `--err` | Only stdout, or only stderr. |
| `--grep <regex>` | Only lines that match the pattern. |

*Terminal output of oxidepm status and oxidepm logs for an errored app*

```text
$ oxidepm status
╭────┬────────┬──────┬─────┬───┬─────────┬──────┬─────┬────────╮
│ id │ name   │ mode │ pid │ ↺ │ status  │ cpu  │ mem │ uptime │
├────┼────────┼──────┼─────┼───┼─────────┼──────┼─────┼────────┤
│  1 │ mailer │ cmd  │ -   │ 3 │ errored │ 0.0% │ 0B  │ 0s     │
╰────┴────────┴──────┴─────┴───┴─────────┴──────┴─────┴────────╯
$ oxidepm logs mailer --lines 3
[2026-10-31 04:11:47.153] cannot reach smtp
[2026-10-31 04:11:47.559] cannot reach smtp
[2026-10-31 04:11:48.362] cannot reach smtp
```

## flush

```sh
oxidepm flush api
```

`flush` truncates the active log files of an app. Rotated files stay. The log contents are lost, so read them first. Log rotation is automatic ([Log files](https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/log-files/)), so flushing to save space is rarely needed. `flush` is a dangerous request: an AI actor cannot make it.

---

# save and resurrect

Write the list of apps that should run, and start them again.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/save-and-resurrect/

## save

```sh
oxidepm save
oxidepm save --force
```

`save` writes `saved.json` from the apps that should be running. It is refused when that would replace a file that lists apps with an empty list (`E_SAVE_WOULD_EMPTY`), unless you pass `--force`. The file is written atomically, with mode 0600, and carries a version number. A file from an older release is refused: run `save` again.

The markers `protected` and `ai_control` are saved too, so `delete all` followed by `resurrect` brings an app back with the markers it had.

## resurrect

```sh
oxidepm resurrect
```

`resurrect` starts the apps that should be running and are not up. An app you stopped stays stopped. It also adds apps from `saved.json` that were deleted since. Apps start the way a config file starts them: in dependency order, with their own result each.

## At boot

[Survive a reboot](https://oxidepm.com/docs/getting-started/reboot/) shows how to start the daemon at boot with `oxidepm startup`.

Both commands are dangerous requests: an AI actor cannot make them. Both take [`--dry-run`](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/dry-run/).

---

# Dry run

Ask what a command would do and change nothing.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/dry-run/

`--dry-run` previews an operation. It is a global flag, and most commands that change something accept it.

*Terminal output of oxidepm stop all --dry-run*

```text
$ oxidepm stop all --dry-run
ℹ Dry run of 'stop': this is what would happen. Nothing was changed.
  stop  web [step 0]  status running
  stop  api [step 1]  status running
  stop  db [step 2]  status running
```

## Which commands

- **The daemon answers with a plan:** `start`, `stop`, `restart`, `reload`, `delete`, `flush`, `save`, `resurrect`, `kill` and `policy set`, and `adapter enable`, `disable` and `remove`. The daemon runs the policy exactly as for the real request, records the rehearsal in the audit log (the lines say `"dry_run": true`), and answers with the apps it would reach, the step each happens in (stop and kill go dependents first), and for a refusal the error code.
- **The command rehearses itself:** `startup`, `update`, `backup` and `restore`, and `adapter import` and `adapter update`. A rehearsal never starts a daemon.
- **Adapters with previews:** `init`, `git-start`, `deploy` and `diff` preview through a running daemon after their adapters are enabled. For example, `oxidepm --dry-run init ./my-project` prints the configuration it would write.
- **Reads:** a command that only reads ignores the flag.
- **Unsupported:** `start --check`, `env set` and `env unset` refuse the flag. The `check`, `web`, `notify` and `monit` adapter commands have no dry run. Use plain `oxidepm check` to report findings without changing the project.

## What a plan is

A daemon plan uses the registry and files to report the intended operations. A rehearsed restart leaves an AI actor's restart allowance intact. Use `--json` for machine-readable output.

A request that the policy refuses is answered with the refusal as the plan (`E_POLICY_DENIED`, `E_PROTECTED`, `E_RATE_LIMITED`). A request that is invalid for a reason the daemon can see without side effects (a bad spec, a missing dependency, an unusable saved file) is answered with the real error.

`update --dry-run` downloads the archive into a private temporary directory, checks it against `checksums.txt`, unpacks it there, shows what it would replace and deletes the directory.

## For agents

An AI actor can use a rehearsal to see what a stop or restart would reach before it asks for it. A rehearsal gives it nothing a `status` does not, and a `start`, `delete`, `save` and the other dangerous requests are refused for it as plans, like the real ones.

---

# JSON output

The --json flag, and what it prints.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/json-output/

Most commands take `--json` and print JSON instead of a table.

*Terminal output of oxidepm --json status*

```text
$ oxidepm --json status
[
  {
    "id": 1,
    "name": "mailer",
    "mode": "cmd",
    "pid": null,
    "restarts": 3,
    "status": "errored",
    "cpu_percent": 0.0,
    "memory_bytes": 0,
    "uptime_secs": 0
  }
]
```

A running app has `"status": "running"`: the table calls it `online`. `tags` is present when the app has any.

## Other output

- `oxidepm --json show <name>` prints the same fields plus the command, working directory, arguments, `last_exit_code`, `healthy` and the two policy markers.
- `oxidepm --json <command> --dry-run` prints the plan: `op`, a `decision`, an `items` list with one entry per app (`id`, `name`, `action`, `detail`, `order`) and `warnings`.
- `oxidepm --json audit` prints one audit record per line.

An error is printed as text, with a non-zero exit code, in `--json` mode too. The stable `E_` code of an error is on the daemon's socket, in the audit log and in the adapter protocol; see [Error codes](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/error-codes/).

---

# Error codes

The stable E_ codes, where you can see them, and what they mean.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/error-codes/

Errors carry a stable name that starts with `E_`. The CLI prints the message, and exits with a non-zero code. The name is what a program should match on. You can see it in the daemon's JSON responses on the socket, in the `deny` part of the [audit log](https://oxidepm.com/docs/ai-safety/audit-log/), and in the [adapter protocol](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/errors/).

A crash loop is not an error code. An app in a crash loop is in the `errored` state. The reason is in the logs and in the daemon's status data.

## Requests and apps

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `E_BAD_REQUEST` | Malformed JSON or an unknown request type. |
| `E_PROTOCOL_VERSION` | The request's protocol is outside the supported range. |
| `E_REQUEST_TOO_LARGE` | A request line over the size limit. |
| `E_INVALID_SPEC` | A spec failed validation. The message names the field. |
| `E_INVALID_NAME` | An app name with a bad charset or length, or a reserved one. |
| `E_INVALID_SELECTOR` | A selector that cannot be parsed or is not allowed for the operation. |
| `E_UNSUPPORTED` | A feature that is not available: removed, or not built yet. |
| `E_APP_NOT_FOUND` | A selector matched nothing. |
| `E_APP_EXISTS` | The name is taken, or the app is already active. |
| `E_BUILD_FAILED` | The build step failed. |
| `E_SPAWN_FAILED` | The program did not resolve or could not be spawned. |
| `E_CANCELLED` | A pending start was cancelled by a stop or delete. |
| `E_SHUTTING_DOWN` | The daemon is shutting down. |
| `E_BUSY` | An app's mailbox stayed full. |
| `E_TIMEOUT` | A bounded wait expired. |

## Dependencies

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `E_DEPENDENCY_MISSING` | A dependency is not registered. |
| `E_DEPENDENCY_CYCLE` | The dependencies form a cycle. The message names it. |
| `E_DEPENDENCY_FAILED` | A dependency is `stopped` or `errored`, or failed while the app waited. |
| `E_DEPENDENCY_TIMEOUT` | The wait for dependencies passed `depends_timeout`. |

## Storage

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `E_DB` | A database error. |
| `E_IO` | A file error. |
| `E_STATE_INCOMPATIBLE` | Stored state was written by an incompatible OxidePM. |
| `E_SAVE_WOULD_EMPTY` | `save` would replace a non-empty file with an empty one. |
| `E_INTERNAL` | A bug, or an internal task died. The daemon log has the details. |

## Policy

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `E_POLICY_DENIED` | The policy refused the request for this actor. The message names the tier, the actor and the apps. |
| `E_PROTECTED` | The app is protected and the actor is not a person. |
| `E_RATE_LIMITED` | A non-human actor asked too often. |
| `E_AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE` | A non-human actor's caution or dangerous request was refused because the audit log could not record it first. |
| `E_DRY_RUN_UNSUPPORTED` | A verb or command has no dry run. |

## Adapters

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `E_ADAPTER_MISSING` | The named adapter or runtime is not imported or not enabled. |
| `E_ADAPTER_UNAVAILABLE` | Enabled but not running, failed, still starting, or its circuit breaker is open. |
| `E_ADAPTER_TIMEOUT` | A call to an adapter timed out. |
| `E_ADAPTER_CRASHED` | The adapter exited during a call. |
| `E_ADAPTER_PROTOCOL` | The adapter broke the protocol, or speaks another version. |
| `E_ADAPTER_BUSY` | The adapter's in-flight limit was reached. |
| `E_ADAPTER_INVALID` | A manifest, plan or name is invalid, or a command collides with a built-in one. |
| `E_ADAPTER_TAMPERED` | The executable's SHA-256 no longer matches the one recorded at import. |
| `E_CHECKSUM_MISMATCH` | A downloaded file does not match the checksum published for it. |
| `E_SIGNATURE_INVALID` | A signature is wrong. |
| `E_INDEX_STALE` | The index is expired or older than the last one seen. |

---

# Other commands

Update, backup and restore, env, top, completions, and the commands that adapters provide: web, monit, init, check, deploy and diff.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/other-commands/

## update

`oxidepm update [--version X] [--force]` updates to a release. See [Upgrade](https://oxidepm.com/docs/getting-started/upgrade/).

## backup and restore

```sh
oxidepm backup --output my-server-backup.tar.gz
scp my-server-backup.tar.gz user@newserver:~
ssh user@newserver "oxidepm restore my-server-backup.tar.gz && oxidepm resurrect"
```

`backup` exports the config and the process list to a tarball. `restore` restores it, and the daemon must not be running. `-y` overwrites existing files without asking. A backup does not include the notifier's configuration, because it holds tokens.

## env

`oxidepm env list <name>` lists the keys of an app's environment. `env set` and `env unset` are refused. See [Environment and hooks](https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/environment-and-hooks/).

## adapter

`oxidepm adapter import`, `list`, `info`, `search`, `enable`, `disable`, `update` and `remove`. See [Import and enable](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/import-and-enable/).

## Commands that come from adapters

On Linux, [build, import and enable the optional adapter](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/import-and-enable/#build-an-optional-adapter) before using its commands. The CLI names the adapter when a command is unavailable. See [Provided by adapters](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/overview/#provided-by-adapters).

## init and check

Import the `init` and `check` adapters to generate a project config and check project readiness.

```sh
oxidepm init ./my-project          # scan a directory and write oxidepm.config.toml
oxidepm check ./my-app             # is the project ready to run?
oxidepm check ./my-app --fix       # install dependencies, create .env
oxidepm start ./my-app --check     # check before starting one app
oxidepm --dry-run init ./my-project
```

`init` detects Node.js, Cargo, Python and Go projects and preserves existing configs. `check` reports on dependencies, lockfiles, environment files and port availability. With `--strict`, warnings make it fail. `--fix` can install Node dependencies and create `.env` from a template, and `--set-env KEY=VALUE` edits `.env`. Both write options are limited to projects within the current directory.

## git-start

The `git-start` adapter prepares a Git checkout in its own state directory and starts it. Use `--offline` to reuse a local checkout or `--no-start` to prepare it without launching. `--install` opts into Node dependency installation. Add `--allow-scripts` to allow dependency lifecycle scripts.

```sh
oxidepm git-start https://github.com/user/repo --branch main
oxidepm --dry-run git-start https://github.com/user/repo
```

## deploy and diff

The `deploy` adapter provides both commands.

```sh
oxidepm deploy user@myserver --cwd /srv/myapp --post "npm run build" --restart api
oxidepm --dry-run deploy user@myserver --cwd /srv/myapp --branch main
oxidepm diff user@myserver --cwd /srv/myapp --count 10
```

`deploy` pulls from `origin` on the remote branch, or the branch selected by `--branch`. It runs the optional `--post` command and restarts processes using the remote `oxidepm` executable, which `--remote-bin` can override. A restart failure returns exit status 3. `diff` shows recent commits, working-tree status and a diff summary. Both use noninteractive SSH and require a known-hosts entry. Both support `--dry-run`.

## File watching

Import and enable the `watch` service on Linux. Add this table to each app you want to restart when its files change:

```toml
[apps.adapters.watch]
paths = ["src"]
ignore = ["generated/*"]
debounce_ms = 200
```

Paths are relative to the app's working directory. If `paths` is omitted, the adapter watches that directory. Your ignore patterns extend the defaults, which include `.git`, `node_modules` and `target`.

## web

Build and import the `ui-web` adapter before using these commands.

```sh
oxidepm web              # where it listens, and its access key (shown once)
oxidepm web new-key      # replace the key
```

The adapter serves a REST API and a WebSocket on `127.0.0.1:9615`. API endpoints other than `/api/health` require the `X-API-Key` header, even on loopback. The first start makes a random key in the adapter's `config.toml`. A browser WebSocket can send it through the `oxidepm-key.<key>` subprotocol alongside `oxidepm.v1`. The adapter validates `Host`. For writes and WebSocket upgrades, `Origin` must be absent or match the configured origin.

With the default `lifecycle` grant, it shows every app and can restart or stop the ones that list `ui-web` under `adapters`. The daemon applies its policy to each request from `adapter:ui-web` and records it in the audit log. Use a TLS reverse proxy when exposing the service outside a trusted network.

| Endpoint | Method | Key | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/api/health` | GET | No | `{"ok":true}`. |
| `/api/processes` | GET | Yes | All apps. |
| `/api/processes/:selector` | GET | Yes | One app. |
| `/api/processes/:selector/stop` | POST | Yes | Stop. |
| `/api/processes/:selector/restart` | POST | Yes | Restart. |
| `/api/processes/:selector/logs` | GET | Yes | Logs. |
| `/api/ping` | GET | Yes | Ask the daemon whether it is alive. |
| `/api/save`, `/api/resurrect` | POST | Yes | Save or start the saved apps. Requires `admin`. |
| `/ws` | WebSocket | Yes | The daemon's lifecycle events as they happen. |

`POST /api/processes` (start an app) and `DELETE` require the `admin` level and return 403 under the default grant. Use the [Prometheus exporter](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/exporter-prometheus/) for `/metrics`.

## monit and top

`oxidepm monit` is the terminal dashboard from the `ui-tui` adapter. It shows app state, CPU and memory, details and logs. It asks for `y` or `n` before stopping or restarting an app. The session needs a terminal for input and output and takes no arguments.

```sh
oxidepm monit
```

`oxidepm top`, a live resource monitor, is still in the core.

## completions and man

```sh
oxidepm completions bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/oxidepm
oxidepm completions zsh > ~/.zfunc/_oxidepm
oxidepm completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/oxidepm.fish
oxidepm man
```

---

# How adapters work

What an adapter is, what runs where, and what happens when one fails.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/how-adapters-work/

## What an adapter is

An adapter is a separate executable that `oxidepmd` starts and supervises. It talks to the daemon over its standard input and output, one JSON-RPC message per line. The protocol is documented, so an adapter can be written in any language. The daemon itself does not fetch anything: importing is done by the CLI.

There are two kinds, named by the `kind` field of the manifest:

- **service**: resident. It starts when you enable it and the supervisor restarts it if it dies. It can subscribe to app events. The notifier, Prometheus exporter, web API (`ui-web`) and `watch` are services.
- **tool**: started on demand to answer a request, kept warm for 30 seconds, then asked to exit. The runtime adapters, the terminal dashboard (`ui-tui`) and commands that run once are tools.

## What an adapter can add

An adapter can listen to lifecycle events, ask the daemon to do things within a grant, add a command to the CLI (the notifier adds `oxidepm notify`, `ui-web` adds `oxidepm web`, `ui-tui` adds `oxidepm monit`), and provide a runtime for apps (`runtime-node`, `runtime-python`, `runtime-go` and `runtime-rust`). The core itself runs only the `cmd` runtime. Whatever it provides is named in its manifest, and is shown before you enable it.

An adapter never starts, stops or changes an app on its own authority. When it asks the daemon, the request goes through the same policy, audit log and rate limits as a person's or an agent's, as the adapter and under the grant you accepted. A request an adapter makes is written to the audit log with its name.

## When one fails

- A crash, a hang, a flood of output or a broken protocol gets the adapter killed and restarted with a growing delay. Three protocol violations in 60 seconds count as a crash.
- Events for a service that is down or slow are dropped and counted, never queued without limit.
- A request to an adapter that is missing, failed or not ready fails with a named error (`E_ADAPTER_MISSING`, `E_ADAPTER_UNAVAILABLE`, `E_ADAPTER_TIMEOUT`, `E_ADAPTER_CRASHED`). There is no silent fallback.
- The daemon never stops, restarts, signals or changes an app because an adapter failed.

## Which adapters exist

The release bundles `runtime-node`, `runtime-python`, `runtime-go` and `runtime-rust`. On Linux, build an archive for any of the optional adapters: `check`, `init`, `git-start`, `deploy`, `watch`, `ui-web`, `ui-tui`, [notifier](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/notifier/) and [exporter-prometheus](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/exporter-prometheus/). See the [adapter list](https://oxidepm.com/adapters/) for what each one provides and the permissions it asks for. AI adapters are unavailable in this release.

## Where they come from

Import an archive by SHA-256 from a file or HTTPS URL, from the release bundle with `oxidepm adapter import --bundled`, or by name with `oxidepm adapter import <name>` when a signed index is configured. This release ships without a configured network catalog. See [Import and enable](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/import-and-enable/).

---

# Import and enable

Install an adapter from an archive you pin, read what it asks for, and enable it.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/import-and-enable/

On Linux, `adapter import` verifies and installs an adapter. `adapter enable` asks you to accept its permissions. Use `import --enable` to do both in one command. Services start when enabled, and tools start when called.

## List

*Terminal output of oxidepm adapter list and list --available*

```text
$ oxidepm adapter list
No adapters are installed. `oxidepm adapter list --available` shows what the index offers.
$ oxidepm adapter list --available
Error: no index is configured in this build. Import by a pinned hash (`oxidepm adapter import <file or url> --sha256 <hex>`) or from the bundle of a release (`oxidepm adapter import --bundled`)
```

`list` shows the installed adapters. `list --available` and `search` require a configured signed index. This release ships without a network catalog.

## Import

An archive is a gzip tarball with `manifest.json` and the executable the manifest names in `exec`, side by side. Import it from a file or an https URL, and pin it with its SHA-256:

```sh
oxidepm adapter import notifier.tar.gz --sha256 <hex> --allow-reserved-name
```

Without `--sha256` nothing is installed: the command prints the archive's hash and asks you to run it again with `--sha256` if you trust it. On a terminal, a pinned import asks you to type the first 12 digits of the hash when it is not given.

For pinned archives that use a reserved name, add `--allow-reserved-name`. That applies to `notifier`, `ui-web`, `ui-tui`, `check`, `init`, `git-start`, `deploy`, `watch` and the runtime adapters. Import `exporter-prometheus` with the digest alone.

`oxidepm adapter import <name>` looks up an adapter in a configured signed index. When the release bundle is installed, `oxidepm adapter import --bundled --tag runtime --enable --yes` verifies its `SHA256SUMS` and imports and enables the bundled runtimes offline. The install script runs this command on Linux.

*Terminal output of oxidepm adapter import*

```text
$ oxidepm adapter import notifier.tar.gz --sha256 fa85a17e321cfbb84e5af87835ea399def9cd0d6670df6f8f16746d0149cb203 --allow-reserved-name
Adapter   notifier 0.1.0 (service)   Telegram, Discord, Slack and webhook notifications.
          Sends a message to the channels you configure when an app starts, stops, restarts, crashes, loops, goes over its memory limit or fails its health check. It reads only those events and its own config.toml, and it never touches your apps.
Source    notifier.tar.gz (pinned by you)
Trust     pinned by you: sha256 fa85a17e321cfbb84e5af87835ea399def9cd0d6670df6f8f16746d0149cb203. Program sha256 d57290e957af80897bea384066311d07cf4bfb1d9da4e314760e35503b85fe77. No signature
Needs     host      read only (status). Events: lifecycle.
          network   outbound. It says it uses api.telegram.org, discord.com, hooks.slack.com. Not enforceable per host.  [BROAD]  Enforced on this machine: yes (seccomp)
          files     writes only its own directory, reads /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/hosts, /etc/nsswitch.conf, /etc/host.conf, /etc/gai.conf.  Enforced on this machine: yes (Landlock 10)
          programs  none.                                                                   Enforced on this machine: yes (Landlock 10)
          environment receives OXIDEPM_TELEGRAM_TOKEN from your environment.  [BROAD]
          memory    128 MiB.
Adds      commands: notify (caution, writes)
Next      oxidepm adapter enable notifier --accept 33926d31eb91080f
Again, what it needs:
  host      read only (status). Events: lifecycle.
  network   outbound. It says it uses api.telegram.org, discord.com, hooks.slack.com. Not enforceable per host.  [BROAD]  Enforced on this machine: yes (seccomp)
  files     writes only its own directory, reads /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/hosts, /etc/nsswitch.conf, /etc/host.conf, /etc/gai.conf.  Enforced on this machine: yes (Landlock 10)
  programs  none.                                                                   Enforced on this machine: yes (Landlock 10)
  environment receives OXIDEPM_TELEGRAM_TOKEN from your environment.  [BROAD]
  memory    128 MiB.
✓ Installed notifier 0.1.0 (disabled, nothing runs). Enable it with: oxidepm adapter enable notifier --accept 33926d31eb91080f
```

Read this before you go on. `Needs` is what the adapter asks for, and `Again, what it needs` repeats it at the end so nothing in the description can push it out of sight. `[BROAD]` marks power that deserves a second look. `Enforced on this machine` says what the operating system can hold the adapter to here. `Trust` says where the archive came from: a pinned archive says `pinned by you` and `No signature`. Nothing runs yet.

## Enable

```sh
oxidepm adapter enable notifier
```

`enable` shows the permissions again and asks for consent. On a terminal you answer the question. In a script, pass `--accept <fingerprint>` with the fingerprint that `import` and `info` print, which ties your consent to exactly that release. `--yes` accepts without asking, only for an adapter that needs nothing broad.

*Terminal output of oxidepm adapter enable: the consent screen*

```text
$ oxidepm adapter enable notifier
Adapter   notifier 0.1.0 (service)   Telegram, Discord, Slack and webhook notifications.
          Sends a message to the channels you configure when an app starts, stops, restarts, crashes, loops, goes over its memory limit or fails its health check. It reads only those events and its own config.toml, and it never touches your apps.
Source    pinned:notifier.tar.gz installed 2026-10-31T04:06:41Z
Trust     pinned by you. Program sha256 d57290e957af80897bea384066311d07cf4bfb1d9da4e314760e35503b85fe77. No signature
Needs     host      read only (status). Events: lifecycle.
          network   outbound. It says it uses api.telegram.org, discord.com, hooks.slack.com. Not enforceable per host.  [BROAD]  Enforced on this machine: yes (seccomp)
          files     writes only its own directory, reads /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/hosts, /etc/nsswitch.conf, /etc/host.conf, /etc/gai.conf.  Enforced on this machine: yes (Landlock 10)
          programs  none.                                                                   Enforced on this machine: yes (Landlock 10)
          environment receives OXIDEPM_TELEGRAM_TOKEN from your environment.  [BROAD]
          memory    128 MiB.
Adds      commands: notify (caution, writes)
Next      oxidepm adapter enable notifier --accept 33926d31eb91080f
Again, what it needs:
  host      read only (status). Events: lifecycle.
  network   outbound. It says it uses api.telegram.org, discord.com, hooks.slack.com. Not enforceable per host.  [BROAD]  Enforced on this machine: yes (seccomp)
```
