```text
  files     writes only its own directory, reads /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/hosts, /etc/nsswitch.conf, /etc/host.conf, /etc/gai.conf.  Enforced on this machine: yes (Landlock 10)
  programs  none.                                                                   Enforced on this machine: yes (Landlock 10)
  environment receives OXIDEPM_TELEGRAM_TOKEN from your environment.  [BROAD]
  memory    128 MiB.
Enable notifier with this grant? [y/N] 
```

If you answer no, nothing is changed:

*Terminal output when the answer is no*

```text
Enable notifier with this grant? [y/N] no
Error: Not enabled
```

If you answer yes:

*Terminal output when the answer is yes*

```text
Enable notifier with this grant? [y/N] yes
✓ Enabled notifier 0.1.0 (level read, scope all)
  Enforced by the OS on this machine: fs_write, fs_read, spawn
```

You can enable with less than the adapter asks for. `--level read` or `--level lifecycle` gives a lower host level, and `--scope opted-in` limits it to the apps that list the adapter. On Linux, `--allow-unenforced` accepts missing sandbox restrictions that the adapter requires. macOS supports the built-in `cmd` runtime. The adapter launcher and sandbox are Linux-only in this release.

## Build an optional adapter

Build an archive from the [adapter sources](https://github.com/oxidekit/oxidepm-adapters). Keep the core checkout in `../oxidepm` so Cargo can find the shared crates. For the `watch` adapter on x86_64 Linux, run these commands in the adapters checkout:

```sh
cargo build --release -p oxidepm-adapter-watch -p oxidepm-adapter-bundle
target/release/oxidepm-adapter-bundle --out target/watch-bundle \
  --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --url-base https://example.org/adapters --sequence 1 \
  watch:target/release/oxidepm-watch
```

Start the daemon with `oxidepm resurrect` if it is down. Use the archive's filename and its digest from `target/watch-bundle/SHA256SUMS`:

```sh
oxidepm adapter import ./target/watch-bundle/watch-0.4.0-rc.1.tar.gz --sha256 <digest> --allow-reserved-name --enable
```

For the other optional adapters, use their directory, executable and digest. The catalog URL is required by the bundle builder. A local pinned import reads the archive directly.

## Look at it, and manage it

*Terminal output of oxidepm adapter info*

```text
$ oxidepm adapter info notifier

          Sends a message to the channels you configure when an app starts, stops, restarts, crashes, loops, goes over its memory limit or fails its health check. It reads only those events and its own config.toml, and it never touches your apps.
Source    pinned:notifier.tar.gz
Trust     pinned by you. Program sha256 d57290e957af80897bea384066311d07cf4bfb1d9da4e314760e35503b85fe77. No signature
Needs     host      read only (status). Events: lifecycle.
          network   outbound. It says it uses api.telegram.org, discord.com, hooks.slack.com. Not enforceable per host.  [BROAD]  Enforced on this machine: yes (seccomp)
          files     writes only its own directory, reads /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/hosts, /etc/nsswitch.conf, /etc/host.conf, /etc/gai.conf.  Enforced on this machine: yes (Landlock 10)
          programs  none.                                                                   Enforced on this machine: yes (Landlock 10)
          environment receives OXIDEPM_TELEGRAM_TOKEN from your environment.  [BROAD]
          memory    128 MiB.
Adds      commands: notify (caution, writes)
Next      fingerprint 33926d31eb91080f
Again, what it needs:
  host      read only (status). Events: lifecycle.
  network   outbound. It says it uses api.telegram.org, discord.com, hooks.slack.com. Not enforceable per host.  [BROAD]  Enforced on this machine: yes (seccomp)
  files     writes only its own directory, reads /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/hosts, /etc/nsswitch.conf, /etc/host.conf, /etc/gai.conf.  Enforced on this machine: yes (Landlock 10)
  programs  none.                                                                   Enforced on this machine: yes (Landlock 10)
  environment receives OXIDEPM_TELEGRAM_TOKEN from your environment.  [BROAD]
  memory    128 MiB.
```

| Command | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `adapter list` | The installed adapters, with state and trust. |
| `adapter info <name>` | Everything about one: state, source, grant, what is enforced, crashes and protocol strikes, and the last lines it wrote to stderr. |
| `adapter disable <name>` | Stop it and take its rights away. |
| `adapter remove <name> [--purge]` | Remove its files. Its state directory is kept unless you pass `--purge`, because it may hold tokens and keys. |
| `adapter update <name>` or `--all` | Update to a newer release. An update that asks for more than the installed one needs `--accept` with the new fingerprint. `--rollback` goes back to the previous version without the network. |

`import`, `update`, `enable`, `disable` and `remove` take [`--dry-run`](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/dry-run/). Enabling, disabling and removing are dangerous requests, so an AI actor cannot make them.

## If the program changes

The SHA-256 of the executable is recorded at import. If it no longer matches when the daemon starts the adapter, the adapter is not started and is marked failed (`E_ADAPTER_TAMPERED`).

---

# Permissions

What a manifest can ask for, and what the daemon enforces itself.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/permissions/

An adapter declares what it needs in the `permissions` object of its manifest. Some of it the daemon enforces itself, some the operating system enforces, and some is only what you consent to.

## The fields

- `host` (object): `level` is `read`, `lifecycle` or `admin`. `scope` is `all` or `opted-in`. Optionally `max_in_flight`, up to 128.
- `events` (list, default: none): The event families a service receives: `lifecycle` and `adapter`. A tool receives no events.
- `env_pass` (list, default: none): Names of environment variables the adapter receives from the daemon's environment. Nothing else is passed.
- `network` (object): `mode` is `none` or `outbound`. `hosts` lists the hosts it says it uses, and `listen` the addresses it listens on.
- `fs` (object): `read` and `write` are lists of paths. `$STATE` is the adapter's own state directory. `any` means any path.
- `spawn` (object): `mode` is `none`, `named` (with `names`) or `any`.
- `memory_mb` (number, default: 128): A memory ceiling, at most 512.
- `requires_enforcement` (list, default: none): Things the OS must enforce, or the adapter is not enabled: `network`, `fs_write`, `fs_read`, `spawn`.

## What the host level allows

`read` makes safe requests: `status`, `show`, `describe`, `logs` and the daemon's status. `lifecycle` also stops, restarts and reloads apps. `admin` also starts apps and makes the dangerous and global requests: `delete`, `flush`, `save`, `resurrect`. Always only on apps that are not protected, and, with scope `opted-in`, only on apps that list the adapter under `adapters`. `kill`, changing policy markers and revealing environment values are a person's, whatever the grant.

## Who enforces what

| Layer | What it enforces |
|---|---|
| The daemon | The host level and scope, the markers, the audit log, the rate limits, the size and rate limits of the protocol, what is in an event, and the scrubbing of an app's secrets from logs. All of it holds whether or not the adapter cooperates. |
| The operating system | Which files it can read and write, which programs it can start, and its system calls. On Linux, through Landlock and seccomp. See [The sandbox](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/sandbox/). |
| You | What you accepted on the consent screen. The list of hosts an adapter says it connects to is shown, but it is not enforced per host. Local Unix sockets (a session bus, an ssh agent) may also stay reachable; see [The sandbox](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/sandbox/). |

## What an update may change

An update that asks for more than the installed version, in any field, shows what grew (`[GROWS]` in the list and a `Grows` section) and needs a new acceptance. Asking for less never needs one.

## Environment values in events

An event never carries an app's command, arguments, working directory, environment, hooks or log lines. `logs` that an adapter reads through the host API are scrubbed of the app's environment values (those of 6 or more characters, by exact match) and bounded at 10 000 lines and 1 MiB.

---

# The sandbox

Landlock and seccomp: what they limit, where they apply and where they stop.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/sandbox/

## What runs

On Linux, `oxidepm-sandbox` sits next to `oxidepmd` and sets restrictions before launching an adapter. It uses Landlock and seccomp where the kernel supports them:

- **Landlock** limits the files the adapter can read and write, and the programs it can start, to what its manifest lists.
- **seccomp** limits the system calls it can make, which is how network use is limited.

`oxidepm status --daemon` shows what this machine can do.

*Terminal output of oxidepm status --daemon*

```text
$ oxidepm status --daemon
audit log:    ok
agent socket: bound
sandbox:      landlock abi 10 (restricts unix connect), seccomp, ptrace_scope 1 (launcher installed)
```

Here Landlock is at ABI 10 (which also restricts connecting to Unix sockets), seccomp is available, `ptrace_scope` is 1 and the launcher is installed. The import and enable screens say, line by line, what is enforced on this machine.

## When it cannot be set up

If the sandbox cannot be set up the way the grant says, the adapter is not started. If the kernel has no Landlock or no seccomp, or the launcher is not installed, the consent screen says `no (this kernel has no Landlock)` or `no (the sandbox launcher is not installed)` for that part. An adapter that requires enforcement is then not enabled, unless you accept that with `--allow-unenforced`.

## What it does and does not do

It limits the damage a buggy adapter can do: it keeps it out of the rest of the file system, and from starting programs it did not declare. It does not fully contain a hostile adapter. In particular:

- Network access is not enforced per host. The manifest names the hosts, and the consent screen says `Not enforceable per host`.
- It does not take back what you approved.
- Local Unix sockets may stay reachable: the session bus, an ssh agent or the display server. `adapter info` prints `AF_UNIX services reachable:` with the ones its self-test could connect to. On a kernel with Landlock ABI 10, which `status --daemon` shows as `restricts unix connect`, this can be closed.
- macOS supports the built-in `cmd` runtime. The adapter launcher and sandbox are Linux-only in this release.

That is why an adapter is also checked against a hash, why you see what it asks for first, and why the daemon enforces the host level on its own. Only install adapters you trust.

---

# The notifier

Telegram, Discord, Slack and webhook notifications.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/notifier/

The notifier is a service adapter. It listens to the lifecycle events of the daemon and sends them to Telegram, Discord, Slack and a signed HTTP webhook. It has read access only and never touches your apps. It also adds the `oxidepm notify` command.

## Install it

On Linux, [build the notifier archive](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/import-and-enable/#build-an-optional-adapter) and use its filename and digest from `SHA256SUMS`. `notifier` is a reserved name.

```sh
oxidepm adapter import ./notifier-0.4.0-rc.1.tar.gz --sha256 <digest> --allow-reserved-name --enable
```

See [Import and enable](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/import-and-enable/). The manifest asks for read access to status and lifecycle events, outbound network (it names `api.telegram.org`, `discord.com` and `hooks.slack.com`), write access only to its own state directory, and the environment variable `OXIDEPM_TELEGRAM_TOKEN`.

## Events

| Event | Severity | When |
|---|---|---|
| `start` | info | An app was started. |
| `stop` | info | An app was stopped. |
| `restart` | warning | An app was restarted: after a crash, by a limit, by cron or by hand. |
| `memory_limit` | warning | An app went over its memory limit and is being restarted. |
| `crash` | critical | An app crashed or ended `errored`. The message has the exit code, the signal or the error text. |
| `crash_loop` | critical | An app crashes again and again and is no longer restarted. |
| `health_check` | critical | A health check failed. |

Messages contain app names, ids, error text and health-check endpoints. Consider that before routing alerts to a shared channel.

## Configure it

The configuration is `config.toml` in the adapter's own state directory. `oxidepm notify status` prints the path. It is not in the home directory, and `oxidepm backup` does not include it because it holds tokens.

*config.toml*

```toml
events = ["crash", "restart"]   # empty or absent: every event
min_severity = "warning"        # info | warning | critical
timeout_secs = 10               # per request, 1 to 60

[telegram]
bot_token_env = "OXIDEPM_TELEGRAM_TOKEN"   # read from the daemon's environment; or bot_token = "..."
chat_id = "-100123456789"

[discord]
webhook_url = "https://discord.com/api/webhooks/..."

[slack]
webhook_url = "https://hooks.slack.com/services/..."

[webhook]
url = "https://example.org/alerts"
secret = "..."   # signs every request
```

A webhook request carries `X-OxidePM-Timestamp` and `X-OxidePM-Signature: v1=<HMAC-SHA256 of "<timestamp>.<body>" with the secret>`. A file that does not parse is an error that `notify status` shows. It is never replaced, and nothing is sent until it is fixed. The file is read again when it changes.

## The notify command

```sh
oxidepm notify telegram --chat YOUR_CHAT_ID    # the token comes from OXIDEPM_TELEGRAM_TOKEN or bot_token, never the command line
oxidepm notify events --set crash,restart,health_check
oxidepm notify severity warning
oxidepm notify test       # sends to every channel whatever the filters say; exits non-zero if one fails
oxidepm notify status
oxidepm notify remove CHANNEL
```

*Terminal output of oxidepm notify status*

```text
$ oxidepm notify status
Notification configuration
Config file: /home/deploy/.oxidepm/adapters/state/notifier/config.toml
Configuration: ok
Telegram: not configured
Discord: not configured
Slack: not configured
Webhook: not configured
Events: all
Minimum severity: none
```

`notify` is a caution-tier command, so an AI actor cannot run it at all, and it is audited. Without the adapter, `oxidepm notify` exits with code 2 and prints `'notify' is provided by the adapter 'notifier', which is not installed.` and the command that imports it.

---

# The Prometheus exporter

Prometheus metrics from the daemon's status, served by an adapter.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/exporter-prometheus/

The exporter is a service adapter with read access only. On each scrape it asks the daemon for the status of the apps, at most once a second however many scrapers there are, and never touches them.

## Install it

On Linux, [build the exporter archive](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/import-and-enable/#build-an-optional-adapter) and use its filename and digest from `SHA256SUMS`.

```sh
oxidepm adapter import ./exporter-prometheus-0.4.0-rc.1.tar.gz --sha256 <digest> --enable
```

The manifest asks for read access to status, to listen on `127.0.0.1:9616`, to read its own state directory, and for outbound network without naming any host; the consent screen marks that last one `[BROAD]`. It serves the Prometheus text format on `/metrics`, and nothing else.

*prometheus.yml*

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: oxidepm
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["127.0.0.1:9616"]
```

## What it exports

*Metrics served by the exporter*

```text
$ curl -s 127.0.0.1:9616/metrics
# HELP oxidepm_up Whether the exporter could read the process list from the daemon (1) or not (0)
# TYPE oxidepm_up gauge
oxidepm_up 1
# HELP oxidepm_processes_total Total number of managed processes
# TYPE oxidepm_processes_total gauge
oxidepm_processes_total 4
# HELP oxidepm_process_up Whether the process is running (1) or not (0)
# TYPE oxidepm_process_up gauge
oxidepm_process_up{name="db",id="1",mode="cmd"} 1
oxidepm_process_up{name="worker",id="4",mode="cmd"} 0
# HELP oxidepm_process_restarts_total Total number of process restarts
# TYPE oxidepm_process_restarts_total counter
oxidepm_process_restarts_total{name="worker",id="4",mode="cmd"} 3
```

That is a part of the real output. The other families are `oxidepm_process_uptime_seconds`, `oxidepm_process_memory_bytes` and `oxidepm_process_cpu_percent`, each per app with the labels `name`, `id` and `mode`. Label values are escaped.

If the daemon cannot be asked (it is stopped, busy, or refused the request), the answer is HTTP 503 with only `oxidepm_up 0`, never an empty list that looks healthy.

## Configuration

An optional `config.toml` in the adapter's state directory, read when the adapter starts. Disable and enable it again after a change.

*config.toml*

```toml
listen = "127.0.0.1:9616"       # an IP address and a port; the default
key = "at least 16 characters"  # required for any address that is not loopback
```

- An address that is not loopback (`0.0.0.0` included) without a `key` is refused: the adapter listens nowhere, and `adapter info` shows why.
- With a key, every request needs `Authorization: Bearer <key>`, and so does a loopback bind that has a key.
- Without a key (loopback only), the `Host` header must be `localhost` or a loopback address with the port that is bound, so a web page whose name was re-pointed at `127.0.0.1` cannot read the metrics.
- There is no TLS. Put a proxy in front of it for anything but a trusted network.
- The sandbox lets the adapter bind the ports its manifest lists, which is 9616 as shipped. Another port needs a build whose manifest lists it, and a new consent at `enable`.

---

# Agent connections

How the daemon decides who is asking, and the agent socket.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/ai-safety/agent-connections/

## Who is asking

The daemon decides who is asking from the connection a request arrives on. What a client writes about itself is only a claim, and a claim can make a request stricter, never looser.

| Where the request comes in | Class | Label |
|---|---|---|
| `daemon.sock`, no claim | human | `cli` |
| `daemon.sock`, claim `human:<label>` | human | the label |
| `daemon.sock`, claim `ai:<label>` | ai | the label |
| `daemon.sock`, any other claim (`adapter:*` and `system:*` may never be claimed by a client, and a label must be 1 to 32 characters of `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -`) | ai | `invalid-claim` |
| `agent.sock`, whatever the claim | ai | the label of an `ai:<label>` claim, otherwise `agent` |

The CLI sends `OXIDEPM_ACTOR` as its claim:

```sh
OXIDEPM_ACTOR=ai:assistant oxidepm status
```

Set it for every agent you run. `OXIDEPM_SOCKET` names the socket the CLI talks to. Pointing an agent at `agent.sock` gives it class `ai` whatever it claims, so it does not depend on the agent being honest about itself:

```sh
OXIDEPM_SOCKET=~/.oxidepm/agent.sock oxidepm status
```

## The agent socket

`agent.sock` is created in the data directory with mode 0600. `agent_socket = false` in `daemon.toml` turns it off. It is tighter than the main socket:

- lines of at most 1 MiB,
- at most 32 connections at once (the 33rd is closed),
- a connection that is idle for 60 seconds is closed,
- a write the client does not read is abandoned after 10 seconds.

If it cannot be bound (a path that is too long, a file in the way), the daemon starts without it and says so in its log.

## What the daemon records

The daemon writes every request to its log with the actor, the class and the socket. Reads are at debug level. The lifecycle events of an app are credited to the actor of the request that caused them, or to `system:crash`, `system:limit`, `system:cron`, `system:health` and `system:resurrect` when the daemon acted on its own.

## What this gives and what it does not

- It binds an AI that goes through the agent socket or that declares itself. It makes a confused or over-eager agent safe.
- It does not stop a hostile or careless process that runs as the same user and calls `oxidepm` without declaring anything. That process reaches the main socket and is a person as far as the kernel can tell. Code that runs as you is you.
- A class decides what a request may do ([Permission tiers](https://oxidepm.com/docs/ai-safety/permission-tiers/)). A refused request is answered `E_POLICY_DENIED` or `E_PROTECTED`, the message names the actor, the request and the apps, and nothing changes.

To contain an agent that runs in a container, run it as the same user inside the container (for example rootless Podman with `--userns=keep-id`), bind-mount only `agent.sock` into it and set `OXIDEPM_SOCKET` to the mounted path. The container then cannot reach `daemon.sock`.

## An adapter that starts the CLI

A process in an adapter's process tree that opens the daemon's main socket itself, for example the CLI started by the adapter, is handled as that adapter under its grant, whatever it claims. The daemon looks at the peer once, when the connection is accepted. A peer that cannot be looked at then is treated as an AI, not as a person.

---

# Permission tiers

Safe, caution and dangerous requests, and what an AI actor may ask for.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/ai-safety/permission-tiers/

Every request has a tier. A person (class `human`, any label) may make every request. An `ai` actor, whether it declared itself or came in on `agent.sock`, is held to the tier.

| Tier | Requests | An `ai` actor |
|---|---|---|
| safe | `status`, `show`, `describe`, `logs`, `ping`, `hello` | Yes, on every app, protected ones too. |
| caution | `stop`, `restart`, `reload` | Only on an app marked `ai_control` and not `protected`. |
| dangerous | `start` (and a config file: a spec is arbitrary code), `delete`, `flush`, `kill`, `save`, `resurrect`, `show --reveal` | Never. |

## Rules for caution requests

- An `ai` actor must name its apps: a name or an id, at most 10. `all` and `@tag` are refused for `stop`, `restart` and `reload`.
- The check is all or nothing. If one app of the request (an instance of a cluster counts) is not open to the actor, nothing runs, and the error names the apps that are not.
- The apps that passed the check are the ones acted on. An app that gains a tag or is created while the request is being checked is not touched.
- `restart` also starts an app that is at rest. That is how an AI brings back what it may control.

*Terminal output of an agent's requests*

```text
agent$ oxidepm stop web --dry-run
ℹ Dry run of 'stop': this is what would happen. Nothing was changed.
  stop  web [step 0]  status running

agent$ oxidepm restart db
✗ ai:assistant may not restart protected app(s): db. A protected app is read-only for anything but a person
Error: ai:assistant may not restart protected app(s): db. A protected app is read-only for anything but a person

agent$ oxidepm delete api
✗ ai:assistant may not make the request 'delete': it is a dangerous request. Ask a person to run it
Error: ai:assistant may not make the request 'delete': it is a dangerous request. Ask a person to run it
```

The CLI prints the message. The code (`E_PROTECTED`, `E_POLICY_DENIED`) is in the [audit log](https://oxidepm.com/docs/ai-safety/audit-log/).

## Rate limits

An `ai` actor can restart or reload the same app once every 10 seconds and five times in ten minutes (`E_RATE_LIMITED`), so a looping agent cannot keep an app down. More generally, a non-human actor is limited to 50 requests a second (a burst of 100), and requests that change something, or are refused for being dangerous, to 5 a minute (a burst of 10). An `ai` actor's allowance is shared by every `ai` actor on the same socket, so changing the label in the claim does not buy a new one.

## What the markers do not limit

The markers limit requests, not the daemon's own work. A crash restart, a `restart_cron` restart, a limit restart and the boot resurrect treat a protected app like any other.

## Adapters

An adapter is held to its [grant](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapters/permissions/) on top of this: `read`, `lifecycle` or `admin`. `kill`, changing the markers and revealing environment values are a person's, whatever the grant.

---

# Protected apps

The protected and ai_control markers, and how to change them.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/ai-safety/protected-apps/

Two markers belong to an app. Both are off by default.

- `ai_control` (boolean, default: false): AI actors may stop, restart and reload the app. Set with `oxidepm start --ai-control`, or `ai_control = true` in the config file.
- `protected` (boolean, default: false): The app is read-only for every non-human actor, whatever `ai_control` says. Set with `--protected`, or `protected = true`.

A protected app can still be read: `status`, `show`, `describe` and `logs` work for an AI actor. A person is never limited by the markers.

*oxidepm.config.toml*

```toml
[[apps]]
name = "db"
mode = "cmd"
script = "postgres"
protected = true

[[apps]]
name = "web"
mode = "npm"
script = "start"
ai_control = true
```

## Change them while the app runs

*Terminal output of oxidepm policy set*

```text
$ oxidepm policy set web --protected
✓ web: protected=true ai_control=true
```

```sh
oxidepm policy set web --protected
oxidepm policy set web --protected=false --ai-control
oxidepm policy set @backend --ai-control=false
```

`policy set` changes the markers of running apps without a restart. At least one of the two flags is required. It is a dangerous request: only a person can make it. An AI cannot protect, unprotect or open an app. `oxidepm status --more` shows the markers in the `policy` column.

- For a cluster, the cluster and every instance change in one transaction. An instance created later takes the markers of its cluster.
- The markers are kept in the database (`state.db`) and in `saved.json`, so they survive a restart of the daemon, and `delete all` followed by `resurrect` brings an app back with the markers it had.
- A `start` of an app that exists keeps its stored markers, whatever the spec or config file says, so running `oxidepm start <file>` again cannot clear `protected`.

## Dry runs

`oxidepm --dry-run policy set web --protected=false` shows the change and makes none:

*Terminal output of oxidepm policy set with --dry-run*

```text
$ oxidepm policy set web --protected=false --dry-run
ℹ Dry run of 'set_policy': this is what would happen. Nothing was changed.
  set_policy  web  protected true -> false, ai_control true -> true
```

Most requests that change something can be rehearsed this way. See [Dry run](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/dry-run/) for the ones that cannot.

---

# Audit log

What is written to the audit log, what is not, and how to read it.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/ai-safety/audit-log/

Everything an AI or an adapter asks for is recorded, and so is every caution or dangerous request by anyone.

## The files

The log is two JSON-lines files in `~/.oxidepm/audit/` (the directory is mode 0700, the files 0600, created when the first line is written):

- `audit.jsonl`: every recorded request.
- `audit-security.jsonl`: the denials, the dangerous requests, and what a non-human actor changed. A chatty but permitted actor cannot rotate this file's evidence away.

Each request leaves a `decision` line (who asked, the operation and its tier, the selector and the apps it reached, `allow` or `deny` with the reason) and, if it ran, a `result` line (`ok`, the error code, how many apps changed or failed, the milliseconds). The two share a `req` number the daemon assigns. The id the client chose is kept as `client_req`. A start also records the program, the number of arguments and a digest of them. `seq` counts up across rotation, so a gap shows a lost line.

*Lines of audit-security.jsonl*

```text
{"v":1,"seq":5,"ts":"2026-10-31T04:21:24.168Z","phase":"decision","req":"r3","client_req":"188ea6-1","actor":{"class":"ai","label":"assistant","via":"agent","pid":1609382,"uid":1001},"op":"restart","tier":"caution","selector":"db","decision":"deny","deny":{"code":"E_PROTECTED","why":"ai:assistant may not restart protected app(s): db. A protected app is read-only for anything but a person"},"dry_run":false}
{"v":1,"seq":6,"ts":"2026-10-31T04:21:24.173Z","phase":"decision","req":"r4","client_req":"188ec7-1","actor":{"class":"ai","label":"assistant","via":"agent","pid":1609415,"uid":1001},"op":"delete","tier":"dangerous","selector":"api","decision":"deny","deny":{"code":"E_POLICY_DENIED","why":"ai:assistant may not make the request 'delete': it is a dangerous request. Ask a person to run it"},"dry_run":false}
{"v":1,"seq":7,"ts":"2026-10-31T04:21:24.177Z","phase":"decision","req":"r5","client_req":"188ee9-1","actor":{"class":"ai","label":"assistant","via":"agent","pid":1609449,"uid":1001},"op":"stop","tier":"caution","selector":"all","decision":"deny","deny":{"code":"E_POLICY_DENIED","why":"ai:assistant may not use 'all' or a tag with 'stop': name the apps"},"dry_run":false}
```

## What is recorded

- Every request of a non-human actor. Repeated `ping`, `hello` and `status` are one line per actor and operation per minute, with a count. `show`, `describe` and `logs` are one line each, with the app, because they are how arguments and logs are read.
- A person's caution and dangerous requests.
- Every denial, whoever asked.

## What is never written

Environment values, hook and probe scripts, the arguments themselves, log lines, the app spec and adapter configuration. The record is a fixed set of fields with no place for them, and free text is cut to a fixed length.

## Written before it runs

A non-human actor's caution or dangerous request is written to disk before it runs. If the log cannot be written (the directory is a file, the disk is full, the writer is stuck), the request is refused with `E_AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE` and nothing happens. A read still goes through, and the lost line is counted. A person is never held up: a stop works while the log is broken, which is how a full-disk incident is handled. The lines that could not be written are counted. `oxidepm status --daemon` shows `audit log: ok` or `degraded`, how many lines were lost, and what is wrong.

## Read it

*Terminal output of oxidepm audit*

```text
$ oxidepm audit --tail 7
2026-10-31T04:21:24.161Z #3      ai:assistant stop [caution] allow web (dry run)
2026-10-31T04:21:24.162Z #4      result r2 ok changed=0 failed=0 0ms
2026-10-31T04:21:24.168Z #5      ai:assistant restart [caution] DENIED E_PROTECTED: ai:assistant may not restart protected app(s): db. A protected app is read-only for anything but a person db
2026-10-31T04:21:24.173Z #6      ai:assistant delete [dangerous] DENIED E_POLICY_DENIED: ai:assistant may not make the request 'delete': it is a dangerous request. Ask a person to run it api
2026-10-31T04:21:24.177Z #7      ai:assistant stop [caution] DENIED E_POLICY_DENIED: ai:assistant may not use 'all' or a tag with 'stop': name the apps all
2026-10-31T04:21:24.183Z #8      human:cli set_policy [dangerous] allow web
2026-10-31T04:21:24.183Z #9      result r6 ok changed=1 failed=0 0ms
```

```sh
oxidepm audit --tail 50
oxidepm audit --actor ai:assistant        # or just `ai`, or just `assistant`
oxidepm audit --op restart
oxidepm audit --since 30m              # or an RFC 3339 time
oxidepm audit --security               # the second file
oxidepm --json audit                   # one JSON object per line
```

`oxidepm audit` reads the files directly, so it works with the daemon down. A request that matches keeps its result line. Every string an actor could have written (labels, reasons, notes) is printed with control characters replaced, so a label cannot move the cursor or paint over the lines around it.

## Rotation and limits

The files rotate at 10 MiB (5 MiB for the security file) and keep ten each. There is no tamper evidence beyond the file mode: a process with your rights can rewrite the files, as it can rewrite the database.

---

# Safe use with AI agents

A runbook: which commands are safe to let an agent run, and the mistakes agents make.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/ai-safety/safe-use/

This is a runbook for letting an AI assistant manage processes through OxidePM. The rule of thumb: **let the AI read freely, and require a person to confirm anything that stops, restarts, deletes or truncates.**

## Commands by risk

**Safe, read-only:** `status`, `show`, `logs`, `env list`, `describe`, `ping`, `top` and `--version`.

**Caution:**

| Command | Notes |
|---|---|
| `start <target>` | Starts a process, or every app of a config file. Check the config first. An app that is already up is refused. |
| `stop`, `restart`, `reload` | Brief downtime. A stopped app stays stopped. |
| `save` | Refuses to replace a non-empty file with an empty list unless `--force`. |
| `startup` | Generates an autostart script. |
| `resurrect` | Starts everything the registry says should run. Verify the saved state first. |
| `check` | The adapter command is caution-tier. `--fix` can install Node dependencies and create `.env`, and `--set-env` can edit `.env`. |
| `deploy` | Pulls code and restarts processes on a remote host. |
| `update` | Replaces the installed binaries and stops a running daemon. |

**Dangerous:** `kill` (stops the daemon and every app), `delete`, `flush` (the log contents are lost), `restore`, `policy set`, and `show --reveal` (its output ends up in the conversation).

Treat `all` as a higher-risk variant of every command that accepts it.

## Mistakes agents make

| Mistake | What happens |
|---|---|
| A wrong `mode` | The process is run with the wrong runtime. |
| Guessed field names | The file is refused and the unknown key is named, so nothing starts. `restart` is the key for the restart mode, not `restart_mode`. |
| `restart = "always"` for a process that exits normally | It is restarted over and over, with a growing delay, until more than `max_restarts` exits fall inside `crash_window`. |
| A very high `max_restarts` | A crash loop can run for a long time. |
| Editing the config while the app runs | The running process keeps the spec it was started with. Stop it, then start the file again. |
| `env set` or `env unset` | Both are refused. Use `--env` or the config file. |
| `--watch` or `watch = true` | The CLI refuses these legacy settings. Use `[apps.adapters.watch]` to [opt in to file watching](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/other-commands/#file-watching). |
| `pkill` or `kill -9` instead of `oxidepm stop` | OxidePM's state no longer matches the real processes. |
| `flush` to clean up | It destroys the diagnostic history. Rotation is already automatic. |
| Restarting an `errored` app without reading its logs | You find the cause first, then restart. |
| `all` when one app was meant | Unrelated services are stopped or deleted. |
| A loop of its own (`while true`, cron, a watcher) | Let OxidePM restart apps. |

## Rules

1. Review a config an AI wrote before it is started. Confirm `mode`, `script` or `bin`, `cwd`, `env`, ports and the restart policy.
2. Confirm before a destructive command: `kill`, `delete`, `flush`, or anything with `all`.
3. Read the logs before you restart. `oxidepm logs <name>` first.
4. Keep secrets out of prompts and configs. `status`, `show`, `describe` and `env list` do not show environment values, but command arguments, URLs, logs and config files are not scrubbed.
5. Put the agent on `agent.sock` and set `OXIDEPM_ACTOR`, so the limits apply whatever it does. Mark the apps it may restart `ai_control`, and the ones it must not touch `protected`.
6. Run `oxidepm describe <name>` after any config change.

## Commands that adapters provide

`web`, `monit`, `notify`, `deploy` and the other commands that [adapters provide](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/overview/#provided-by-adapters) are caution or dangerous requests, and they go through the same policy and audit log as every other command. A session command such as `monit`, which takes over a terminal, is refused for an AI actor unless its adapter says it may be driven by one.

## The web API

The `ui-web` adapter listens on `127.0.0.1` by default and requires an access key for its API, with an exception for `/api/health`. The default grant shows all apps and permits stops and restarts only for apps that list `ui-web` under `adapters`. Keep the access key private. The daemon applies policy to requests from `adapter:ui-web` and records them in the audit log.

---

# Overview

Protocol version 1: transport, framing and the rules every message follows.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/overview/

This is how `oxidepmd` talks to an adapter: an executable it starts and supervises. This is protocol version 1. The examples on these pages are the reference frames that the daemon, its test adapter and the protocol crate's own tests all read. Changing one is a protocol change and needs a new protocol number.

## Transport and framing

- The adapter's standard input carries daemon to adapter, and its standard output adapter to daemon. Both are UTF-8, one JSON object per line, ended by `\n`. A frame never contains a raw newline.
- Each object is a JSON-RPC 2.0 message with these restrictions:
  - `"jsonrpc":"2.0"` is required. There are no batches: an array is a violation.
  - `id` is an unsigned 64-bit integer. Each side numbers its own requests from 1 and never reuses a number.
  - `params` and `result` are objects. A missing `params` means `{}`.
  - `method` is 1 to 64 characters of letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`.
  - A response has `result` or `error`, never both. An error is `{code: integer, message: string, data?}`.
  - A line that is empty, contains a NUL byte or is not valid UTF-8 is not a frame.
- Unknown fields are ignored. An unknown request method is answered with error `-32601`. An unknown notification is ignored.
- Standard output carries protocol and nothing else. Standard error is the adapter's log: lines are cut at 8 KiB, rate limited to 1 MiB per second, kept in the adapter's own rotated file (1 MiB, 5 files) and never mixed into the daemon's log.

## The environment

The adapter is started with a cleared environment: a short base (`PATH`, `LANG`, `HOME` set to its state directory), the names its manifest lists in `env_pass`, and `OXIDEPM_ADAPTER_PROTOCOLS`, the comma-separated protocol numbers the daemon speaks. A process that finds that variable missing was not started by the daemon.

## Kinds

`service` is resident and receives events. `tool` is started on demand and exits when idle. The kind is set in the manifest and sent in `initialize`.

## Where to read on

- [Messages](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/messages/): every method.
- [Handshake and lifecycle](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/lifecycle/): starting, checking and stopping.
- [The host API](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/host-api/): how an adapter asks the daemon to act.
- [Events](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/events/): what a service is told.
- [Limits and timeouts](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/limits/) and [Errors](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/errors/).
- [Write an adapter](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/write-an-adapter/): the manifest and the archive.

---

# Messages

Every method the daemon and an adapter may send.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/messages/

## Daemon to adapter: requests

The adapter answers each with a `result` or an `error`.

| Method | Params | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `initialize` | `protocols`, `host`, `adapter`, `kind`, `grant`, `paths`, `limits` | `{protocol, name, version}` |
| `ping` | `{}` | `{}`. Sent every 15 seconds to a service. |
| `shutdown` | `{}` | `{}`. Sent when the adapter is stopped. |
| `runtime.prepare` | `spec`, `path_hint`, `phase` (`start` or `restart`) | `{steps, notes}` |
| `runtime.plan` | `spec`, `steps_done` | `{program, args, cwd, extra_env, binary_path}` |
| `command.invoke` | `verb`, `argv`, `cwd`, `dry_run`, `actor`, `tty` | `{exit_code, result?}` |

`runtime.prepare` and `runtime.plan` are how a runtime adapter launches an app while the core still owns the child. The adapter returns data: build steps (an `id`, an `argv`, a `cwd`, extra environment, a timeout, whether to capture output, and whether the step is optional), and then a launch plan (a program, arguments, a working directory and extra environment). The core checks and runs the steps in their own process group and spawns the plan itself. The adapter runs nothing. The `spec` it sees is a redacted view: the keys of the environment with the value `<redacted>`.

*runtime.prepare and its reply*

```text
daemon:  {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"runtime.prepare","params":{"spec":{"name":"web","runtime":"node","command":"server.js","args":["--port","3000"],"cwd":"/srv/web","tags":["prod"],"ports":[3000],"instances":1,"env":{"DATABASE_URL":"<redacted>"},"options":{"node_args":["--max-old-space-size=512"]}},"path_hint":"/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin","phase":"start"}}
adapter: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"result":{"steps":[{"id":"install","argv":["npm","ci"],"cwd":"/srv/web","env_add":{"CI":"1"},"timeout_secs":600,"capture":"none","capture_max":65536,"optional":true,"description":"Install dependencies"}],"notes":["lockfile found"]}}
```

`command.invoke` runs a command that an adapter added to the CLI. The `actor` is the class and label of whoever asked. The `init` adapter supports dry runs and returns the generated configuration.

*command.invoke and its reply*

```text
daemon:  {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":6,"method":"command.invoke","params":{"verb":"init","argv":[],"cwd":"/srv/web","dry_run":true,"actor":{"class":"human","label":"cli"},"tty":false}}
adapter: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":6,"result":{"exit_code":0,"result":{"path":"/srv/web/oxidepm.config.toml","config":"[[apps]]\nname = \"web\"\nmode = \"npm\"\nscript = \"start\"\ncwd = \".\"\n","written":false}}}
```

## Daemon to adapter: notifications

No answer.

| Method | Params |
|---|---|
| `initialized` | `{}` |
| `event` | `{seq, kind, family, at, app?, data, options?, dropped_before?}`. See [Events](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/events/). |
| `cancel` | `{id}`: the request with that id was abandoned, and a late answer will be dropped. |

## Adapter to daemon

| Method | Kind | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `host.request` | request | Asks the daemon to do something. See [The host API](https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/host-api/). |
| `host.audit_note` | request | Writes a line to the audit log: `{"text": "..."}`. |
| `invoke.output` | notification | Streams output of a `command.invoke`: `{id, stream, text}`, with `stream` one of `stdout`, `stderr` or `status`. |
| `cancel` | notification | `{id}`. Accepted and ignored. |

The `provider.*` and `gate.*` method names are reserved.

---

# Handshake and lifecycle

How an adapter starts, is checked and is stopped.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/lifecycle/

## The handshake

The daemon speaks first. The adapter stays silent until it receives `initialize`; a frame sent before that is a violation.

*initialize and its reply*

```text
daemon:  {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocols":[1],"host":{"name":"oxidepmd","version":"1.2.3"},"adapter":{"name":"notifier","version":"0.1.0"},"kind":"service","grant":{"level":"read","scope":"all"},"paths":{"state":"/home/u/.oxidepm/adapters/state/notifier"},"limits":{"max_line":262144,"max_in_flight":32,"event_queue":1024}}}
adapter: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"protocol":1,"name":"notifier","version":"0.1.0"}}
daemon:  {"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"initialized","params":{}}
```

The version numbers in this example are illustrative. The daemon puts its own version in `host.version`.

- The adapter must answer within 10 seconds, with the highest protocol it shares with `protocols`, and its own `name` and `version`.
- The daemon compares `name` and `version` with what it has on record. A difference means the executable is not what was installed: the adapter is killed and marked failed (`tampered`) and does not start again.
- A protocol that is not in the offered list, or an error `-32022` (optionally with `data.supported`), marks the adapter failed (`incompatible`).
- After a good reply, the daemon sends the notification `initialized`. A `service` then receives events. A `tool` is idle until a request arrives.
- A silent or broken handshake ends the process. It counts as a crash, and the supervisor restarts it with a growing delay until it gives up.

*A reply that refuses the protocol*

```text
adapter: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"error":{"code":-32022,"message":"unsupported protocol","data":{"supported":[1],"code":"E_ADAPTER_PROTOCOL"}}}
```

## Staying alive

A service is sent `ping` every 15 seconds and has 5 seconds to answer. Three misses in a row kill it. A tool is not pinged: it is started for a request, kept warm for 30 seconds, and asked to exit when idle.

*ping*

```text
daemon:  {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"ping","params":{}}
adapter: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{}}
```

## Timeouts and cancellation

- Every wait for an adapter is a timer in the daemon. The adapter's cooperation is not needed.
- When a deadline passes, or the caller goes away, the daemon forgets the request at once, sends `cancel {id}` and remembers the id. A reply with that id (a late answer, or error `-32024` from an adapter that obeyed the cancel) is dropped and counted, without a strike. An id that was never issued is a strike.
- When the connection ends for any reason, every request in flight fails with `E_ADAPTER_CRASHED`.

## Shutdown

When the adapter is stopped, the daemon sends `shutdown` and waits up to 2 seconds. It then closes the adapter's standard input (the adapter must also exit when its input closes), waits until 2 seconds are over, sends SIGTERM to the adapter's process group, waits until 5 seconds are over in all, and then sends SIGKILL. The total is fixed. Queued events are written first, for up to a second.

---

# The host API

How an adapter asks the daemon to do something, and what the grant allows.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/host-api/

An adapter reaches the daemon through `host.request` and nothing else. `params.request` is the object the CLI would send, for example `{"type":"stop","selector":{"by":"name","value":"web"}}`. `params.dry_run` asks for a plan instead of the action. A request that only reads ignores it. `params.end_user` is an optional label of at most 64 characters, with control characters removed, for the adapter's own end user. The answer's `result.response` is the daemon's response, exactly as the CLI would get it.

*host.request and its reply*

```text
adapter: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"host.request","params":{"request":{"type":"stop","selector":{"by":"name","value":"web"}},"dry_run":true}}
daemon:  {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"response":{"type":"error","code":"E_POLICY_DENIED","message":"denied"}}}
```

## The daemon decides who is asking

- The request is handled as the adapter, named by the connection, under the grant the user accepted when the adapter was enabled. Nothing the adapter writes can change that. An `actor`, `reveal`, `dry_run` or any other field inside the request object, or extra fields in `params`, is not read. Only `request`, `dry_run` and `end_user` are taken from `params`.
- The request goes through the same policy, audit log and dry-run handling as a request from the CLI. A refusal is a normal response (`type: "error"`, with `E_POLICY_DENIED`, `E_PROTECTED`, `E_RATE_LIMITED`, `E_SHUTTING_DOWN` and so on), not a protocol error. Denied requests are written to the audit log with the adapter's name.
- The `end_user` label is written to the audit log as an unverified label. It is never used in a decision.

## What a grant allows

- `read`: safe requests (`status`, `show`, `describe`, `logs`, the daemon's status).
- `lifecycle`: also stops, restarts and reloads apps.
- `admin`: also starts apps and does the dangerous and global requests (`delete`, `flush`, `save`, `resurrect`).

All only on apps that are not protected, and, if the grant's scope is `opted-in`, only on apps that list the adapter under `adapters`. `kill`, `set_policy` and revealing environment values are a person's, whatever the grant.

## Logs and size

`logs` for an adapter are scrubbed of the app's environment values (those of 6 or more characters, an exact-match filter) and bounded: at most 10 000 lines and 1 MiB, the newest lines kept. An answer that would not fit in a frame is replaced by `E_REQUEST_TOO_LARGE`.

## Rates

32 requests in flight (the grant may ask for up to 128; the next one is answered with `E_ADAPTER_BUSY`, `-32029`). 50 requests a second with a burst of 100, and 5 requests that change something a minute with a burst of 10 (`E_RATE_LIMITED`). An adapter answered with `E_RATE_LIMITED` 20 times within 10 seconds commits a violation. A `params` that is not a request answers error `-32602`, and that is not a violation.

## Audit notes

`host.audit_note` takes `{"text": "..."}` and writes a line to the audit log, tagged with the adapter's name and cut at 256 characters. It counts against the same rate, and a note is dropped, not waited for, when the log's queue is full.

*host.audit_note*

```text
adapter: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"host.audit_note","params":{"text":"sent a message"}}
```

---

# Events

The lifecycle and adapter event families, and how delivery works.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/events/

Events go to a running `service` that listed the family in its manifest and was granted it. There are two families.

## lifecycle

Something happened to an app. `seq` is the daemon-wide sequence number of the event.

`kind` is one of `started`, `restarted`, `stopped`, `crashed`, `errored`, `unhealthy`, `recovered`, `backoff`, `crash_loop`, `cron_fired`, `memory_limit` and `uptime_limit`.

`app` is `{id, name, tags}`. `data` holds only these keys, and only those the event has: `cause`, `actor`, `pid`, `exit_code`, `exit_signal`, `restarts`, `memory_mb`, `limit_mb` and `reason`. `reason` is a sentence made by the daemon with the app's environment values removed and cut at 1024 characters.

`options` is the app's `adapters.<adapter name>` table for this adapter only, at most 4 KiB. No other adapter's options are ever sent.

The event never carries the app's command, arguments, working directory, environment, hooks or log lines.

*An event*

```text
daemon: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"event","params":{"seq":17,"kind":"crashed","family":"lifecycle","at":"2026-11-20T10:00:00Z","app":{"id":3,"name":"web","tags":["prod"]},"data":{"exit_code":1,"restarts":2},"options":{"chat":"ops"},"dropped_before":4}}
```

## adapter

Something happened to an adapter: `started`, `exited`, `killed` or `failed`. It has no `app`, has its own `seq` counter, and `data` holds `adapter`, `version` and, for `failed`, `reason` (a short name). An adapter is not told about itself.

## Delivery

Delivery is best effort and never slows the daemon. Each service has a queue of 1024 events plus 256 critical ones (`crashed`, `errored`, `unhealthy`, `crash_loop` and `memory_limit`; `killed` and `failed` for the adapter family), at most 4 MiB. When it is full, the oldest normal event is dropped, or the oldest critical one when the critical part is full.

A service that is not running does not queue: its events are dropped. The drops are counted, and the next event delivered carries `dropped_before: n`. A gap in `seq` shows where. Events queued when the process ended are dropped, not sent to the next process. When the adapter is stopped on request, queued events are written, for up to a second, before `shutdown`.

An event line is at most 16 KiB. If one would be longer, the daemon removes `options`, then `reason`, then the tags. If it still does not fit, it is dropped and counted.

---

# Limits and timeouts

The numbers the daemon enforces, and what happens when an adapter exceeds them.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/limits/

All of these are enforced by the daemon. None depends on the adapter's cooperation. They are constants of the protocol version, not configuration.

| What | Limit | When exceeded |
|---|---|---|
| A line, adapter to daemon | 256 KiB | Skipped without being stored. A violation. |
| A frame the daemon would send | 256 KiB | A request is refused before it is sent (`E_ADAPTER_INVALID`). An answer to an adapter's request that is too large is replaced by `E_REQUEST_TOO_LARGE`. |
| An `event` line | 16 KiB | Trimmed. |
| Requests in flight, each direction | 32 (up to 128 for `host.request`, when the grant asks) | The new request fails at once (`-32029`, `E_ADAPTER_BUSY`). |
| Frames from the adapter | 500 a second sustained, burst 1000; 8 MiB a second | The daemon stops reading, so the adapter blocks on its own pipe. Throttled for 10 seconds without a break is a violation. |
| A write to the adapter's input | No progress for 5 seconds | The connection is closed and the adapter killed. |
| Strikes | 3 in 60 seconds | The adapter is killed and counts as a crash. |
| Expired request ids remembered | 1024, for 5 minutes | A late reply with such an id is dropped without a strike. |
| `initialize` | 10 seconds | The adapter fails the handshake. |
| `ping` | 5 seconds to answer | Three misses in a row kill a service. |

## What is a violation

A violation, also called a strike, is: a line that is not a valid frame, an oversize line, a frame before `initialize`, a response to an id that was never issued or was already answered, a reply that does not have the shape of its method, or being throttled too long.

An adapter request with bad params is not a violation. It gets an error. A line that ends the stream half way, an end of file, or a read error closes the connection.

---

# Errors

Error codes in the protocol, and what fails closed or open.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/errors/

An error response is `{code, message, data?}`. `data.code` is the stable name.

## Numeric codes

The numeric codes are the JSON-RPC ones, and those of OxidePM's own range.

| Code | Meaning | Name |
|---|---|---|
| `-32700` | Parse error | |
| `-32600` | Invalid request | |
| `-32601` | Method not found | |
| `-32602` | Invalid params | |
| `-32603` | Internal error | |
| `-32022` | Unsupported protocol | `E_ADAPTER_PROTOCOL` |
| `-32023` | Permission denied | `E_POLICY_DENIED` |
| `-32024` | Cancelled | |
| `-32025` | Timeout | `E_ADAPTER_TIMEOUT` |
| `-32026` | Shutting down | |
| `-32027` | Dry run unsupported | `E_DRY_RUN_UNSUPPORTED` |
| `-32028` | Rate limited | `E_RATE_LIMITED` |
| `-32029` | Busy | `E_ADAPTER_BUSY` |

*A permission error*

```text
daemon: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"error":{"code":-32023,"message":"outside the grant","data":{"code":"E_POLICY_DENIED"}}}
```

The other stable names are listed under [Error codes](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/error-codes/).

## What fails closed

The operation does not happen:

- The executable's SHA-256 differs from the one recorded at install: it is not started (`E_ADAPTER_TAMPERED`).
- The handshake names another adapter or version, or no common protocol: the adapter is killed and marked failed.
- A request to an adapter that is missing, failed or not ready fails with a named error. There is no silent fallback.
- A frame that is not valid, too large or out of turn is never acted on.
- The sandbox cannot be set up as the grant says: the adapter is not started.

## What fails open

The daemon carries on:

- Events to a service are dropped, and counted, when its queue is full or it is down.
- An adapter that crashes, hangs, floods or breaks the protocol is killed and restarted with backoff. The apps the daemon supervises are not touched.
- Unknown fields, unknown notifications and floods on standard error are ignored or dropped.

The daemon never stops, restarts, signals or changes an app because an adapter failed.

---

# Write an adapter

The manifest file, the archive layout and a minimal adapter.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/adapter-protocol/write-an-adapter/

## The archive

An adapter is a gzip tarball with two files at its top level: `manifest.json`, and the executable that the manifest names in `exec`. `exec` must be a relative path, with no `.` or `..` components. The executable must be a native program for the machine it runs on.

```text
notifier.tar.gz
├── manifest.json
└── oxidepm-notifier
```

## The manifest

`manifest.json` declares who the adapter is and what it asks for. It is validated at import and again at every load in the daemon. This is the whole manifest of the Prometheus exporter:

*manifest.json*

```json
{
  "schema": 1,
  "name": "exporter-prometheus",
  "version": "0.4.0-rc.1",
  "kind": "service",
  "summary": "Prometheus metrics for the apps OxidePM manages.",
  "description": "Serves /metrics in the Prometheus text format on 127.0.0.1:9616. On each scrape it asks the daemon for the status of the apps (read access only) and never touches them. It listens on loopback unless its config.toml says otherwise, and any other address needs an access key in that file. If the daemon cannot be reached the answer is HTTP 503 and oxidepm_up 0.",
  "tags": ["exporter"],
  "protocol": [1],
  "min_daemon": "0.1.0",
  "exec": "oxidepm-exporter-prometheus",
  "provides": {},
  "permissions": {
    "host": {"level": "read", "scope": "all"},
    "events": [],
    "env_pass": [],
    "network": {"mode": "outbound", "hosts": [], "listen": ["127.0.0.1:9616"]},
    "fs": {"read": ["$STATE"], "write": []},
    "spawn": {"mode": "none"},
    "memory_mb": 64,
    "requires_enforcement": []
  }
}
```

- `schema` (number): Always `1`.
- `name` (string): 2 to 32 characters. Start with a lowercase letter and use lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. Names such as `core`, `oxidepm`, `oxidepmd`, `all`, `adapter`, `daemon`, `cmd`, `system` and `host` are reserved. See [Import and enable](/docs/adapters/import-and-enable/) for the rules on official adapter names.
- `version` (string): A semantic version.
- `kind` (string): `service` or `tool`.
- `summary` (string): One line, at most 120 characters. Required.
- `description` (string, default: empty): At most 4096 characters. It is shown on the consent screen, followed by the permissions again so it cannot push them out of sight.
- `tags` (list, default: none): At most 10, for listing and search.
- `protocol` (list of numbers): The protocol versions the adapter speaks. At least one must be one the daemon speaks.
- `min_daemon` (string): The oldest daemon version it works with.
- `exec` (string): The executable, relative to the archive.
- `provides` (object, default: empty): `runtimes`, `verbs`, `serves`, `programs`, `capture_programs` and `env_set`.
- `permissions` (object): What it asks for. See [Permissions](/docs/adapters/permissions/).

## Verbs and runtimes

`provides.verbs` adds commands to the CLI. Each has a `name` (2 to 24 characters), a `summary`, a `tier` (`safe`, `caution` or `dangerous`), a `mode` (`relayed` or `session`), whether it `writes`, whether it supports `dry_run`, `max_runtime_secs` (1 to 3600, 600 by default) and an `args_summary`. A verb must not collide with a built-in command or another adapter's verb. A verb that writes cannot be `safe`, and an adapter that may spawn programs or use the network cannot declare a `safe` verb.

`provides.runtimes` names runtimes the adapter provides (a tool only, and never `cmd`), and then must list `provides.programs`, the bare program names it runs.

A `service` may list events, and provides no runtimes. A `tool` receives no events.

## What you write

The program reads one JSON object per line on standard input, and writes protocol on standard output and logs on standard error. It waits for `initialize`, answers it, handles `ping`, and exits on `shutdown` or when standard input closes. A service then handles `event` notifications, and may call `host.request` within its grant. The frames on these pages are the reference.

The [adapter sources](https://github.com/oxidekit/oxidepm-adapters) include `oxidepm-adapter-sdk`, a Rust crate that handles the handshake, `ping`, events, relayed verbs and `shutdown`.

## Try it

```sh
oxidepm adapter import ./my-adapter.tar.gz --sha256 <hex>
oxidepm adapter enable my-adapter
oxidepm adapter info my-adapter
```

`--allow-reserved-name` is only needed for a reserved name. `adapter info` shows the last lines the adapter wrote to standard error, its crashes and its protocol strikes.

---

# OxidePM and PM2

What each process manager is for, where each is the better choice, and the real differences.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/compare/oxidepm-and-pm2/

## In short

PM2 and OxidePM do the same everyday job: they start your apps, restart them when they crash, keep their logs, show a status table and bring the apps back after a reboot. PM2 is written in JavaScript, runs on Node.js and has been used for a long time, especially for Node.js apps. OxidePM is a process manager written in Rust, for Linux, that is young and smaller on purpose, and it adds limits for letting AI agents work with it.

For details about PM2, see the [PM2 documentation](https://pm2.keymetrics.io/docs/usage/quick-start/).

## What each is for

- **PM2** is a process manager for Node.js, and it also runs scripts in other languages. It is a good fit when your stack is Node.js and you want clustering, zero-downtime reloads and a large ecosystem around it.
- **OxidePM** is a process manager for Linux servers whatever the app is written in. It is a good fit when you want one small native daemon that supervises processes, strict config checking, scripting output, and limits on what an AI agent may do to your processes.

## Where PM2 is the better choice

- **Zero-downtime reload for Node.js.** PM2's cluster mode can reload workers one after another so that the app keeps answering. OxidePM has no zero-downtime reload: `reload` is the same as `restart`.
- **Built-in file watching.** PM2 can restart an app when its files change. OxidePM provides file watching through the [`watch` adapter](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/other-commands/#file-watching) on Linux.
- **Windows.** PM2 runs on Windows. OxidePM does not support Windows.
- **Age and community.** PM2 has been in use for years. OxidePM is new and its current release is a release candidate.
- **Deploy and hosted monitoring.** PM2 has its own deploy tooling and an optional hosted monitoring service. OxidePM provides SSH deployments through the [`deploy` adapter](https://oxidepm.com/docs/commands/other-commands/#deploy-and-diff).
- **One shared port for a Node.js cluster.** PM2 cluster mode lets Node.js workers share one port. OxidePM clusters give instance `i` the port `port + i`, so you put a reverse proxy or load balancer in front.

## Where OxidePM is the better choice

- **A native manager with no JavaScript runtime.** The OxidePM daemon and CLI are Rust programs. Running them does not need Node.js on the machine. You install the runtimes your apps need, and nothing else.
- **Limits for AI agents.** The daemon decides who is asking from the connection a request arrives on. An agent on the agent socket may read everything, may only stop or restart apps you opened to it, and can never start, delete or flush. Apps can be marked `protected`, and what agents ask for is written to an audit log. See [Safe use with AI agents](https://oxidepm.com/docs/ai-safety/safe-use/).
- **Rehearsals.** Most commands that change something take `--dry-run`, which answers with a plan and changes nothing.
- **Strict configuration.** A config file with an unknown key, a bad cron expression or a dependency cycle is refused as a whole, with the line of the problem, before anything starts.
- **A crash-loop breaker and a dependency wait that fails closed.** An app that restarts too often ends as `errored` until a person starts it, and an app that waits for `depends_on` fails if its dependencies never come up.
- **A small core and checked adapters.** Notifications, metrics, the web API, the dashboard and the language runtimes are adapters: separate programs that are hash-checked, show what they ask for before you enable them and, on Linux, run under Landlock and seccomp.
- **Machine-readable output.** `--json` on commands and stable `E_` error codes.

## The real differences

| | PM2 | OxidePM |
|---|---|---|
| Written in | JavaScript, runs on Node.js | Rust, native programs |
| Platforms | Linux, macOS and Windows | Linux. macOS supports the built-in `cmd` runtime. The adapter launcher and sandbox are Linux-only in this release. |
| Languages of the apps | Node.js first, other interpreters by script | Any program with `cmd`. Node.js, Python, Go and Rust through runtime adapters that a release carries |
| Reload | Zero-downtime reload for cluster mode | `reload` is a restart |
| Cluster | Node.js workers can share one port | Up to 256 instances, a port each |
| Watch mode | Built in | `watch` adapter |
| Config file | A JavaScript ecosystem file, or JSON | TOML, YAML or JSON, checked strictly |
| Restart policy | Restart on crash, with options | `on-crash`, `always` or `never`, backoff that doubles up to a cap, and a crash-loop breaker |
| Health checks | None built in. An app can signal readiness during a reload | HTTP, TCP or a script, with a choice of action |
| Start order | No dependency option: start order is up to you | `depends_on`, which waits and fails closed |
| Boot | `pm2 startup` and `pm2 save` | `oxidepm startup`, `save` and `resurrect` |
| Dashboard | `pm2 monit` | `oxidepm top` in the core, and `oxidepm monit` from the `ui-tui` adapter |
| Notifications and metrics | Modules and a hosted service | The notifier and Prometheus exporter adapters |
| AI agent limits | None that are built for it | Agent socket, tiers, protected apps and an audit log |
| Licence | AGPL-3.0 | MIT or Apache-2.0 |

## Moving from PM2

The commands map closely.

| PM2 | OxidePM |
|---|---|
| `pm2 start app.js` | `oxidepm start app.js` |
| `pm2 start ecosystem.config.js` | `oxidepm start oxidepm.config.toml` |
| `pm2 list` | `oxidepm status` |
| `pm2 logs api` | `oxidepm logs api -f` |
| `pm2 restart api` | `oxidepm restart api` |
| `pm2 reload api` | `oxidepm reload api`, which is a restart |
| `pm2 stop api`, `pm2 delete api` | `oxidepm stop api`, `oxidepm delete api` |
| `pm2 save`, `pm2 resurrect` | `oxidepm save`, `oxidepm resurrect` |
| `pm2 startup` | `oxidepm startup systemd` |
| `pm2 monit` | `oxidepm monit` (needs the `ui-tui` adapter) |

A PM2 ecosystem file is JavaScript, and OxidePM does not read it. Write the same apps as a [config file](https://oxidepm.com/docs/configuration/config-file/) in TOML, YAML or JSON. Apps that run on Node.js need the `runtime-node` adapter, which a release carries. [Install](https://oxidepm.com/docs/getting-started/install/#runtimes) shows how it is enabled.

## Using both

Nothing stops you from running both on one machine for different apps. Keep each app under one manager only.

Next: [OxidePM and systemd](https://oxidepm.com/docs/compare/oxidepm-and-systemd/).

---

# OxidePM and systemd

Where systemd is enough, where a process manager is easier, and how the two work together.

Source: https://oxidepm.com/docs/compare/oxidepm-and-systemd/

## In short

systemd is the init system and service manager of most Linux distributions. OxidePM is a process manager written in Rust for the apps you run on a server. They are not rivals so much as two layers: `oxidepm startup systemd` writes a systemd unit so that the OxidePM daemon starts at boot, and the daemon then supervises your apps.

systemd alone is often enough to supervise apps. A dedicated process manager can make app operations more convenient.

## What each is for

- **systemd** starts the machine and the services that belong to it: the database, the web server, the system's own daemons. It orders them, isolates them, limits their resources and logs them. It is on almost every Linux server already, and a unit file for your own app is a normal way to run it.
- **OxidePM** supervises the applications of a user or a team, started and stopped from a command line without root, described in one config file, with a status table, and with limits for AI agents.

## Where systemd is the better choice

- **It is already there.** There is no second daemon to install, update or monitor.
- **System services and boot order.** `After=`, `Requires=` and targets order services across the whole machine, including mounts, networks and sockets. OxidePM's `depends_on` orders only the apps that OxidePM supervises.
- **Isolation and resource control.** Each service runs in its own control group. Memory and CPU limits (`MemoryMax=`, `CPUQuota=`), filesystem and privilege hardening (`ProtectSystem=`, `NoNewPrivileges=` and more) and killing every process of a service are systemd features. OxidePM signals the app's process group, and a child that starts its own session or detaches itself is not in it.
- **Socket activation and timers.** Starting a service on the first connection, and scheduled jobs, belong to systemd.
- **Logs.** journald collects the output of every service, with the same tools for all of them.
- **Restarts and rate limits.** `Restart=`, `RestartSec=` and `StartLimitBurst=` cover a crash and a crash loop, and the watchdog can restart a service that stops answering.

## Where OxidePM is the better choice

- **No root, and one command per app.** `oxidepm start app.js` runs as your user, and you do not write a unit file for every app or reload systemd after each change.
- **A status table and a config file for a group of apps.** `oxidepm status` shows every app with its state, restarts, CPU, memory and uptime, and one TOML, YAML or JSON file describes the group.
- **Health checks that act.** An app can be probed over HTTP, over TCP or with a script, and the daemon can restart it when the probe fails. systemd has no HTTP probe of its own.
- **Backoff, a breaker and a dependency wait that fails closed.** Restart delays that double up to a cap, an app that ends as `errored` instead of looping, and `depends_on` that fails if the dependency never comes up.
- **The same tool on a developer's Mac.** macOS supports the built-in `cmd` runtime. The adapter launcher and sandbox are Linux-only in this release.
- **Limits for AI agents.** An agent on the agent socket is held to what you allow, `protected` apps cannot be changed by it, and the audit log records what it asked for. See [Safe use with AI agents](https://oxidepm.com/docs/ai-safety/safe-use/).
- **Rehearsals and JSON.** `--dry-run` on most commands that change something, and `--json` for scripts.

## The real differences

| | systemd | OxidePM |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Init system and service manager, process 1 | A daemon you start per user, which supervises apps |
| Needs root | For system services. User units exist as well | No |
| How an app is described | A unit file | A config file, or flags to `oxidepm start` |
| Stopping an app | Kills every process in the service's control group | Signals the app's process group |
| Resource limits | Control groups, for memory, CPU and more | Memory and uptime limits that restart the app |
| Logs | journald | Per-app files, rotated by size (10 MB and 5 files by default) |
| Ordering | Across the whole system | Between the apps OxidePM supervises |
| Health checks | A watchdog the service must feed | HTTP, TCP or script probes |
| Boot | It is the boot | `oxidepm startup systemd` writes a unit for the daemon, and `resurrect` restores the apps |
| AI agent limits | None that are built for it | Agent socket, tiers, protected apps and an audit log |

## Using them together

The usual setup is both. systemd starts `oxidepmd` at boot through the unit that `oxidepm startup systemd` generates, so that the daemon comes back after a reboot, and OxidePM keeps the apps running. Keep the database and the system's own services as systemd units, and the apps you deploy and restart often under OxidePM. Keep each app under one manager only. See [Survive a reboot](https://oxidepm.com/docs/getting-started/reboot/).

Next: [OxidePM and PM2](https://oxidepm.com/docs/compare/oxidepm-and-pm2/).

---

# Adapters

On Linux, import the bundled runtimes or build and import an archive for an optional adapter. Details: https://oxidepm.com/adapters/

- `notifier` (built): Sends a message to Telegram, Discord, Slack or a signed webhook when an app starts, stops, restarts, crashes, loops, goes over its memory limit or fails a health check. Adds the notify command.
- `exporter-prometheus` (built): Serves /metrics in the Prometheus text format on 127.0.0.1:9616. On each scrape it asks the daemon for the status of the apps, and answers 503 with oxidepm_up 0 when it cannot.
- `ui-web` (built): Serves a REST API and a WebSocket on 127.0.0.1:9615 by default. Shows apps and can stop and restart opted-in apps. API requests require an access key except for /api/health. Adds the web command.
- `ui-tui` (built): The terminal dashboard: the apps with state, CPU and memory, the selected app in detail and its log. Stopping or restarting an app asks for y or n first. Runs only while the dashboard is open. Adds the monit command.
- `runtime-node` (built): Runs Node.js apps: the node, npm, pnpm and yarn runtimes. It tells the daemon what to run and the daemon runs it.
- `runtime-python` (built): Runs Python apps, in the project's virtualenv when it has one. Provides the python runtime.
- `runtime-go` (built): Runs Go apps with go run. Provides the go runtime.
- `runtime-rust` (built): Builds and runs Rust apps: a single file with rustc, a project with cargo. Provides the rust and cargo runtimes.
- `check` (built): Check project readiness with oxidepm check. Use start --check to opt in to preflight for a single target.
- `init` (built): Scan a project and generate oxidepm.config.toml with oxidepm init.
- `git-start` (built): Clone or update a Git checkout and start it with oxidepm git-start.
- `deploy` (built): Pull code and restart services with oxidepm deploy. Inspect the remote checkout with oxidepm diff.
- `watch` (built): Restart opted-in apps when files change under the paths set in apps.adapters.watch.
- `AI adapters` (planned): AI adapters are unavailable in this release.
